weeks.title: Professional communication
weeks.context:
A remote operator lives or dies by the words they send. Nobody sees you work. They see your emails, your messages, your meeting notes, and your follow-through, and from those few signals they decide whether you are someone they can hand real responsibility to. This week is the foundation the whole track stands on, because every later skill (calendar, research, project management, support) is delivered through communication.

You will be working for Ama Mensah, founder of Kola, an Accra-based e-commerce startup that sells handmade West African goods and ships across the region. Ama is busy, a little disorganised, and drowning in messages. Your job this week is to become the person whose emails she trusts without re-reading. By Friday you will have a reusable Communication Toolkit (your own templates) and three real executive emails written on Ama's behalf, the first pieces of your portfolio.

The bar for this week is simple: a stranger should be able to read anything you send and know, in ten seconds, what it is about and what they need to do.

concept_check.q: Ama asks you to 'handle the supplier' and then hears nothing from you for three days. What single habit would most reduce her growing anxiety?
choices: Working faster so it is finished sooner
Sending a short status update so she knows where it stands
Waiting until it is fully done so you do not bother her
Copying her on every email you send to the supplier
concept_check.explain: A brief status update removes the worry. Silence makes a founder assume the worst. Closing the loop is the cheapest trust you can build, and it is the heart of this week.

concept_check.q: Two emails land in a busy inbox. Which gets actioned first: one titled 'Question' or one titled 'Refund policy: customer waiting, need your call by 2pm'?
choices: 'Question', because it is shorter
'Refund policy...', because it states the topic and the deadline
They are treated the same
Neither, both look like spam
concept_check.explain: A specific subject with the topic and a deadline gets prioritised. Vague subjects like 'Question' get skipped because the reader cannot tell what they are for.

concept_check.q: A customer is furious that their order is two weeks late. What should the FIRST move in your reply be?
choices: Explain that the courier caused the delay
Quote the shipping policy
Acknowledge their frustration and that the delay is not okay
Offer a refund and end the conversation
concept_check.explain: People need to feel heard before they can hear a solution. Lead with acknowledgement, then act. Quoting policy or blaming the courier escalates the anger.

days.title: What the job really is, and set up your workspace
days.summary: Understand what a remote operator is paid for, then set up the professional identity you will use for the whole track.

items.title: What a remote operator actually does
items.body:
## The job in one sentence
A remote operator (virtual assistant, executive assistant, operations coordinator, the title changes, the work does not) takes work off a busy person's plate so that person can do the thing only they can do. Ama can design products and talk to suppliers. She cannot also answer 60 emails, book 4 meetings, chase 3 invoices, and keep the team's tasks straight. That second list is your list.

## What you are actually paid for
Not hours. Not tasks completed. You are paid for **reliability and judgement**. A founder is handing you access to their inbox, their calendar, sometimes their money. The thing they are buying is the feeling of *I do not have to check whether this got done.* Everything in this track builds toward earning that feeling.

Here is the part most people miss: almost all of that trust is built through writing. You will rarely be in the same room as the people you work for. They form their entire opinion of you from your messages. A clear, calm, well-structured email tells them *this person has it handled.* A vague, rambling one tells them *I am going to have to double-check everything this person touches.* Same work, opposite outcome, decided by the words.

## Case study: two assistants, same task
Ama asks two assistants to follow up with a supplier who is late on a delivery.

Assistant A sends: *"Hi, just checking on the order, any update? Thanks."*

Assistant B sends: *"Hi Kwesi, following up on PO-114 (50 woven baskets), due last Friday the 6th. Could you confirm a new ship date by end of day tomorrow? If it will slip past the 15th, let me know and I will adjust our store listing. Thank you, Ama's team."*

Both 'did the task'. But B named the order, stated the original deadline, asked for one specific thing by a specific time, and signalled what happens next. Ama can forward B's email without editing it. She has to rewrite A's. After a week of this, B gets handed bigger things and A gets micromanaged. That gap is the whole career.

## This week's destination
By Day 7 you will own a small library of templates for the messages you will send a hundred times (status update, follow-up, scheduling, saying no, apologising), plus three polished emails written for Ama. You are not learning 'how to email'. You are building the assets that make you fast and consistent under pressure.

items.title: What is Virtual Assistance? (Full Tutorial)
items.creator: The Virtual Savvy
items.why: A clear, honest overview of what remote assistant work actually involves day to day: the services, the clients, the reality. Watch it once for the big picture, then come back and build your own setup below.

items.title: Set up your operator workspace, step by step
items.body:
## Do this now, before any lessons
Every client judges you in the first few seconds, from things that have nothing to do with talent: your email address, your signature, your photo. Get these right once and you never think about them again.

**1. A clean email address.** If your only address is something like `coolguy_232@...`, create a new one: `firstname.lastname@gmail.com` or as close as you can get. Go to Gmail, create the account, done. This is the address you will put on your CV and send client work from.

**2. An email signature.** In Gmail, go to Settings (gear icon) > See all settings > General > Signature > Create new. Keep it plain text:

```text
Your Name
Remote Operations Assistant
your.email@gmail.com
```

No images, no inspirational quotes, no five phone numbers. When you save and send yourself a test email, the signature should appear at the bottom automatically. That is the result you want to see.

**3. A profile photo.** A clear, friendly headshot against a plain wall. Phone camera is fine. Good light, face visible, no sunglasses. Set it as your Google account photo so it shows up next to your emails.

**4. Your Communication Toolkit doc.** Open Google Docs, create a blank doc, title it `Communication Toolkit - Your Name`. Paste in five headings now, each on its own line: `Status Update`, `Follow-Up`, `Scheduling`, `Saying No`, `Apology / Bad News`. You will fill these in across the week. This single doc becomes portfolio piece number one.

Everything here is free. No paid tools required this week.

cards.prompt: A remote operator is mostly paid for completing as many tasks as possible.
cards.whenRight: Correct. You are paid for reliability and judgement, the feeling that things are handled without supervision. Volume without trust just gets you micromanaged.
cards.whenWrong: Not quite. Task volume is easy to fake and easy to get wrong. What clients actually buy is not having to check your work, and that comes from reliability and judgement.

cards.prompt: Assistant B's email worked because it named the order, gave a deadline, and asked for one specific thing.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Specifics (which order, the original deadline, one clear ask, by when, what happens next) are what make a message forwardable without edits.
cards.whenWrong: Look again. B won because of specifics: the order number, the original due date, a single clear ask, a deadline, and the next step. That is the whole difference.

cards.prompt: A messy email address like coolguy_232@ is fine as long as your work is good.
cards.whenRight: Right. The client sees the address before they ever see your work. It is a free, two-minute fix that changes their first impression.
cards.whenWrong: It is not fine. People judge the address in half a second, before any of your work is visible. Spend two minutes and make a clean one.

items.title: Your turn, set up your identity
items.body:
Complete the setup. Tick each box only when it is actually done.

- [ ] Created a clean, professional email address (firstname.lastname@ style)
- [ ] Set a plain-text Gmail signature (name, role, email) and sent yourself a test email to confirm it appears
- [ ] Set a clear headshot as your Google account photo
- [ ] Created a Google Doc titled `Communication Toolkit - Your Name` with the five section headings
- [ ] Shared the Toolkit doc with view access so a mentor could open it

Deliverable: a screenshot of your new signature on a test email, and the link to your (currently empty) Toolkit doc.

days.title: Writing that respects the reader's time
days.summary: Learn BLUF and the three-pass edit so a busy person can act on your message in seconds.

items.title: BLUF: Bottom Line Up Front
items.body:
## The reader is skimming. Write for that.
Ama reads your message on her phone, between two other things, while walking. She is not going to study it. If your main point is buried in paragraph three, she will miss it, and then you will both lose a day to the back-and-forth that follows.

The fix is a habit the military, journalism, and consulting all independently arrived at: **Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF)**. Put the most important thing, the decision, the ask, the answer, in the first sentence. Then the supporting detail underneath, in case they want it.

## Before and after
Buried version:

> *Hi Ama, I hope you are well. I have been looking into the printing options for the new packaging like you asked. There were a few vendors and I compared their prices and turnaround times, and one of them is closed next week for a holiday, which complicates things a bit. Anyway, after all that I think we should go with Accra Print Co because they are cheaper and faster. Let me know what you think.*

BLUF version:

> *Recommendation: use Accra Print Co for the new packaging. They are 20% cheaper and 3 days faster than the other two vendors. One catch, our second choice is closed all next week, so if you want a backup we should decide today. Details below.*

Same information. But Ama can act on the second one in five seconds, and the detail is there if she wants it. The first one makes her do the work of finding the point.

## The three-pass edit
Good writing is rewriting. Before you send anything that matters, run three fast passes:

1. **Point pass.** Is my main message in the first line? If not, move it there.
2. **Cut pass.** Delete every word that does not change the meaning. "I just wanted to quickly reach out to see if maybe" becomes "Could you". "At this point in time" becomes "now". Hedging words (just, maybe, sort of, I think) make you sound unsure, cut most of them.
3. **Action pass.** Is it obvious what the reader should do next, and by when? If there is an ask, it should be impossible to miss.

This takes under a minute once it is a habit, and it is the single biggest upgrade to how seriously people take you.

cards.prompt: BLUF means saving your recommendation for the end so the reader follows your reasoning first.
cards.whenRight: Right. BLUF is the opposite: the bottom line goes first, supporting detail after. Busy readers skim, so lead with the point.
cards.whenWrong: Flip it. Bottom Line Up Front means the conclusion or ask comes first. Reasoning lives underneath for anyone who wants it.

cards.prompt: Words like 'just', 'maybe', and 'I think' usually make a message stronger.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Those are hedges. A few are fine for tone, but a pile of them makes you sound unsure. The cut pass removes most.
cards.whenWrong: Other way around. Hedging words weaken you. Trim them in the cut pass so your ask reads as confident, not tentative.

items.title: Rewrite three rambling messages
items.body:
Below are three messages an assistant actually sent Ama. Rewrite each one using BLUF and the three-pass edit. Aim to cut the length by at least a third while making the point clearer.

1. *"Hey! So I was thinking about the customer who emailed about the broken vase, and I am not totally sure what our policy is on refunds versus replacements, and I did not want to promise the wrong thing, so I was wondering if maybe you could let me know how you usually like to handle these kinds of situations when you get a chance? No rush!"*

2. *"Hi Ama, just a quick update, things are going okay on the supplier side, I have been in touch with a couple of them and waiting to hear back from one, the other one replied but I need to double check something before I can confirm, will keep you posted."*

3. *"Hello, I wanted to reach out regarding the Instagram posts for next week because I had some ideas and also a question about whether we are still doing the discount thing and if so when, let me know your thoughts whenever."*

Paste your three rewrites into your Toolkit doc under a new heading "BLUF practice". Then write one sentence on what was wrong with each original.

days.title: The anatomy of a professional email
days.summary: Subject lines, structure, tone, and the cc/bcc/reply-all rules that separate pros from amateurs.

items.title: Every part of an email, done right
items.body:
## The subject line is the email
Half of whether your email works is decided before it is opened. A subject line should let the reader know the topic and urgency without opening it. Compare "Question" with "Refund policy question, customer waiting, need answer today". The second one gets handled first.

Rules: be specific, front-load the keyword, and if there is a deadline, put it in. Update an existing thread's subject when the topic changes instead of replying to a three-week-old chain about something else.

## The structure that always works
1. **Greeting.** "Hi Ama," is right for almost everyone. "Dear Mr Owusu," for first contact with someone senior and formal. Get the name spelling right, every time.
2. **One-line context or BLUF.** Why you are writing.
3. **The body.** Short paragraphs. If there is more than one point, use a numbered or bulleted list. Walls of text do not get read.
4. **A clear ask.** One sentence, ideally with a deadline: "Could you approve this by Thursday so I can place the order?"
5. **Sign-off.** "Thanks," / "Best," then your name. Consistent, simple.

## Tone: warm and competent
You are aiming for warm and competent at the same time. Too cold ("Per my last email, the deadline was Friday.") reads as hostile. Too soft ("sooo sorry to bother you again!!") reads as junior. The middle is plain, friendly, direct: "Quick reminder the deadline is Friday, let me know if you need more time."

## cc, bcc, and reply-all, the rules that save your reputation
- **cc** (carbon copy): everyone sees who is on it. Use for people who need visibility but not action. Putting a founder's name in cc on a vendor email quietly signals authority.
- **bcc** (blind carbon copy): recipients cannot see the bcc list. Use it to introduce two people and then "move someone to bcc" so their inbox is spared the rest of the thread. Never use bcc to secretly loop someone in on a sensitive conversation, if it surfaces, it looks like a betrayal.
- **reply-all**: the classic career landmine. Before you hit it, ask: *does every single person on this thread need my reply?* Usually the answer is no, and you should just reply to one person. Accidentally reply-all-ing "sounds good!" to 40 people is how you become a cautionary tale.

## A small thing that signals a pro
Attachments: mention the attachment in the body ("Invoice attached") and actually attach it before you hit send. The "oops, here is the attachment" follow-up is a tiny credibility leak you can simply stop doing by attaching first, writing second.

items.title: How to Write a Professional Email [STEP-BY-STEP BUSINESS EMAIL]
items.creator: Adriana Girdler
items.why: A tight, practical walk through a real business email: structure, tone, sign-off. Watch how short and scannable she keeps it, then write yours the same way in the exercise.

items.title: Grammarly blog
items.why: A solid free reference for tone, grammar, and phrasing. Browse the business-writing posts, and install the free browser extension so it catches your typos before a client does.

items.title: Write five subject lines and one full email
items.body:
Part 1. Write a specific, scannable subject line for each of these situations:
1. Asking Ama to approve a $300 ad budget by Friday.
2. Telling the team a Monday meeting moved to Tuesday 10am.
3. Following up with a supplier who has not replied in 4 days.
4. Sending a customer their refund confirmation.
5. Flagging that the website has been down for 20 minutes (urgent).

Part 2. Write the full email for situation 1 (the ad-budget approval), using the five-part structure. Keep it under 120 words. Save both parts in your Toolkit doc under "Email anatomy practice".

days.title: Managing up and asking good questions
days.summary: Status updates that build trust, expectation-setting, and the art of the well-formed question.

items.title: Managing up: making your boss's life easy
items.body:
## The status update is your trust machine
The fastest way to make a founder relax is the unprompted status update. When Ama does not hear from you, her brain fills the silence with worry: *did that get done? should I check?* A short, regular update removes that worry, and removing worry is the whole job.

A good update has three parts, often called **Done / Doing / Blocked**:

> *Quick Friday update:*
> *Done: shipped all 12 orders, replied to every customer email, booked the supplier call for Tuesday.*
> *Doing: building the September content calendar, will share Monday.*
> *Blocked: need your okay on the $300 ad budget before I can launch the campaign.*

Three lines. Ama now knows exactly where everything stands and the one thing she needs to do. Send one of these at a regular rhythm (end of day, or end of week) and you will be considered reliable before you have done anything heroic.

## Set expectations before they are violated
Amateurs go quiet when something will be late and hope no one notices. Pros flag it early: *"Heads up, the report will be ready Thursday morning, not Wednesday as I said, the data export took longer than expected. Still fine for the Friday meeting."* A deadline you reset in advance is professionalism. A deadline you blow in silence is a broken promise. Same delay, completely different read.

## Asking a good question
You will need answers from busy people constantly. A bad question creates work: "What should I do about the customer complaint?" forces Ama to think from scratch. A good question does the thinking for her and leaves a simple decision:

> *"Customer says her order arrived damaged. I see two options: (a) full refund, or (b) free replacement plus a 10% discount on her next order, which keeps her as a customer. I lean toward (b). Okay to proceed?"*

Notice the pattern: state the situation, offer options you have already thought through, give your recommendation, ask for a yes/no. This is the single most valuable communication habit in this entire track. It turns you from someone who needs managing into someone who removes decisions from your boss's plate. Do this consistently and you will be handed real authority fast.

cards.prompt: If a deadline is going to slip, the professional move is to stay quiet and try to catch up before anyone notices.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Flag it early. A deadline reset in advance is professionalism, a deadline blown in silence is a broken promise.
cards.whenWrong: No. Silence is the amateur move. Flag the slip early with a new date and the impact. Resetting in advance protects trust, hoping no one notices destroys it.

cards.prompt: A good question includes the situation, options you have already considered, and your recommendation.
cards.whenRight: Yes. That format turns a question that creates work into a simple yes/no decision, which is exactly what busy people want from you.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Situation plus options plus your recommendation plus a simple ask is the high-value pattern. It removes a decision from your boss instead of adding one.

items.title: Write a status update and three good questions
items.body:
Part 1. Imagine your week for Ama looked like this: shipped 8 orders, answered customer emails, drafted next week's social posts (waiting on her review), the photographer cancelled so product photos are delayed, and you need her to confirm whether to reorder the best-selling tote bag. Write a Done / Doing / Blocked update.

Part 2. Turn each of these vague questions into a good question (situation + options + recommendation + simple ask):
1. "What do I do about the supplier who keeps being late?"
2. "How should I respond to the negative Instagram comment?"
3. "Should we offer free shipping or not?"

Save both in your Toolkit doc under "Managing up".

days.title: Hard conversations
days.summary: Saying no, apologising, and turning an angry customer into a calm one, in writing.

items.title: Saying no, apologising, and defusing anger
items.body:
## Saying no without burning the bridge
You cannot say yes to everything, and trying to is how you miss real deadlines. The skill is declining in a way that keeps the relationship warm. The shape is: acknowledge, decline clearly, offer an alternative.

> *"I would love to get this out today, but I am finishing the supplier orders that ship this afternoon. I can have it to you first thing tomorrow, or if it is urgent I can pause the orders, your call."*

That is a no, but it shows you are protecting priorities (which Ama wants) and it hands her the decision. "No" with a reason and an option is a sign of competence, not difficulty.

## The real apology
Everyone makes mistakes. The thing that separates pros is the recovery. A weak apology is all feelings: "I am so so sorry, I feel terrible, this is so embarrassing." That makes the other person comfort *you*. A strong apology is brief, takes ownership, and moves straight to the fix:

> *"That is on me, I sent the wrong invoice. The correct one is attached. I have added a second check to my process so it does not happen again. Sorry for the confusion."*

Own it, fix it, prevent it, move on. No grovelling. People trust someone who handles their own mistakes cleanly far more than someone who never admits one.

## Defusing an angry customer
When someone is angry, they want two things before they want a solution: to feel heard, and to feel like a human is on it. Lead with that. The pattern is **acknowledge, apologise for the experience, act**:

> *"Hi Fatou, you are right to be frustrated, an order three weeks late is not okay and I am sorry. Here is what I am doing right now: I have located your parcel (it is in Tema, out for delivery tomorrow), and I am refunding your shipping fee today. I will personally confirm once it is delivered. Thank you for your patience."*

Notice what is missing: no defensiveness, no "our policy states", no blaming the courier. You can acknowledge a bad experience without admitting legal fault. The angry customer who is handled well often becomes the most loyal one, because most companies handle them badly and you did not.

## The 24-hour rule for your own anger
Sometimes a client or customer is rude and you will want to fire back. Do not send that email. Write it if it helps, then delete it. Wait, even an hour, then reply calm and professional. You will never regret the calm version. You will always regret the heated one, and in writing it lives forever.

items.title: Transforming Difficult Customer Encounters: A Powerful De-escalation Strategy
items.creator: Myra Golden
items.why: Myra Golden trains support teams at large companies. This five-minute strategy for calming an upset person is exactly what you will use on the angry-customer exercise, and again in Week 7.

cards.prompt: A strong apology spends most of its words on how terrible and embarrassed you feel.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Long apologies make the other person comfort you. Strong ones are brief: own it, fix it, prevent it, move on.
cards.whenWrong: No. Excessive feeling forces the other person to reassure you. The strong version takes ownership briefly and gets straight to the fix and the prevention.

cards.prompt: With an angry customer, you should lead by explaining your policy and why the delay was not your fault.
cards.whenRight: Right. Defensiveness and policy-quoting escalate anger. Lead with acknowledgement and a concrete action; the person wants to feel heard and see a human acting.
cards.whenWrong: Other way. Leading with policy or blame makes it worse. Acknowledge the experience, apologise for it, and show the concrete action. Solutions land better after the person feels heard.

items.title: Defuse a real angry email
items.body:
A customer sends Kola this email:

> *"This is ridiculous. I ordered a gift for my mother's birthday TWO WEEKS ago and it still hasn't arrived. No updates, nothing. Her birthday was yesterday. I want my money back and I'm telling everyone I know not to buy from you. Absolutely unacceptable."*

Write the reply, using acknowledge / apologise for the experience / act. Assume you checked and the parcel is genuinely delayed in transit but will arrive in 2 days. Decide what you can offer (refund of shipping, a discount, a small gift) and make it concrete. Keep it under 150 words and human, not corporate.

Then write a second message: a polite 'no' to Ama, who has asked you to also start managing her personal Instagram on top of your current workload. Save both under "Hard conversations" in your Toolkit.

days.title: Meetings, async, and being reliable
days.summary: Agendas, meeting notes, async vs sync, time zones, and the quiet habits that make you trusted.

items.title: Meeting etiquette and the reliability habits
items.body:
## Meetings: your job is to make them worth it
As an operator you will run and attend a lot of calls. The professional handles three moments around every meeting:

**Before:** send an agenda. Even three bullet points ("1. Approve September budget, 2. Decide on new courier, 3. AOB") transforms a meeting from a ramble into a decision-making session. No agenda often means no point.

**During:** be early, test your audio, mute when not speaking, and take notes. If you are running it, keep it on time. If you said 30 minutes, end at 30 minutes, people remember who respects their calendar.

**After:** send notes within an hour, while it is fresh. The format that matters: **Decisions made** and **Action items (who does what, by when)**. The conversation fades from memory by tomorrow, your notes become the record everyone relies on. The person who sends crisp post-meeting notes quietly becomes the most important person in the room.

## Async vs sync: know when not to meet
Remote work runs on a choice: should this be a meeting (sync) or a message (async)? A good rule: if it is a simple update or a question with a clear answer, write it, do not schedule a call. Meetings are expensive (everyone stops working), so reserve them for things that genuinely need discussion: decisions with trade-offs, brainstorming, anything emotional or sensitive. Suggesting "this could be an email" at the right moment makes you look senior.

## Time zones: the remote operator's daily reality
You may work for someone in London, New York, or Dubai while sitting in Accra. Always confirm times with a zone: "3pm GMT" not just "3pm". Learn to convert quickly, and use a tool like Google Calendar (which shows the other person's time) or a world clock. Getting a time zone wrong and missing an international client's call is a brutal first impression you can simply avoid by always stating the zone.

## The quiet habits that build a reputation
None of these are glamorous, all of them compound:
- **Reply to acknowledge, even if you cannot act yet.** "Got it, I will have this done by Thursday" stops the other person wondering if you saw the message.
- **Do what you said you would do, by when you said.** This one habit outranks talent.
- **Close the loop.** When a task is done, say so. Silence after "can you handle X?" leaves people anxious.
- **Be findable and on time.** Boring, decisive. The reliable person gets the opportunities the brilliant-but-flaky person never will.

cards.prompt: Sending meeting notes with clear decisions and action items is one of the highest-leverage things an operator does.
cards.whenRight: Yes. The conversation fades by tomorrow, your notes become the record. The person who writes them becomes quietly indispensable.
cards.whenWrong: It really is. Memory of a meeting fades fast; the written decisions and action items are what the team actually runs on afterward.

cards.prompt: When working with an international client, writing '3pm' without the time zone is fine because they will figure it out.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Always state the zone ("3pm GMT"). A missed call from an ambiguous time is an avoidable, brutal first impression.
cards.whenWrong: No. Always include the zone. '3pm' means different things in Accra, London, and New York, and a missed international call over it is entirely avoidable.

items.title: Run a meeting on paper
items.body:
Ama wants a 30-minute team call to plan the December holiday sale. Produce the three artefacts a professional would create around it:

1. **The agenda** (sent the day before). 3-5 bullet points with a rough time for each, plus the meeting goal in one line.
2. **The meeting notes** (sent after). Invent a realistic set of decisions and write them up as: Decisions made, and Action items in the format "[Owner] will [task] by [date]".
3. **An async judgement call.** Ama also asks "should we hop on a call to discuss the new packaging colours?" Write a one-line reply suggesting whether this should be a call or a message, and why.

Save all three under "Meetings" in your Toolkit doc.

days.title: Channels: email, chat, and voice
days.summary: Choose the right tool for each message and set response-time norms a client can rely on.

items.title: The right channel for the message
items.body:
## Email is not the only channel
Modern remote work runs across several channels, and using the wrong one is a quiet way to annoy people. The operator who picks the right channel for each message looks effortless.

- **Email** is for anything that needs a record, reaches people outside the team (clients, suppliers, customers), or is not urgent. It is async by default: a reply within a few hours is normal, not instant.
- **Chat (Slack, Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp)** is for quick internal back-and-forth, fast questions, and informal coordination. It feels instant, but it is still not a phone, do not expect a reply in 30 seconds, and do not send 'hi' then wait (write the whole question in one message).
- **Voice notes and short videos (Loom)** are underused and powerful. A 60-second voice note or a 2-minute Loom screen recording can explain something that would take ten typed messages. Many busy founders prefer a voice note they can play while walking. Use them to walk someone through a document, show a bug, or give warm feedback.
- **A call** is for decisions with trade-offs, anything emotional or sensitive, and the occasional relationship check-in. Default to async; reserve calls for when they genuinely beat typing.

## The 'one message' rule for chat
On chat, put the whole thing in one message. Compare:

> *Bad: "Hi" ... (waits) ... "are you there?" ... (waits) ... "so about the supplier..."*

> *Good: "Hi Ama, quick one: Northern Weavers can ship the baskets Friday but want 50% upfront. Okay to pay the deposit, or should I push back? No rush, anytime today is fine."*

The good version respects that the other person is busy and lets them answer whenever they look.

## Set response-time expectations
Trust comes from predictability. Tell a new client how you work: "I check email at 9am and 4pm GMT and reply within the day. For anything urgent, message me on WhatsApp." Now they never wonder if you saw something. A client who knows your rhythm is a calm client. A client guessing whether you are awake is an anxious one, and anxious clients micromanage.

## A note on tone across channels
Chat is more casual than email, but 'casual' still means clear and respectful. Emojis are fine on internal chat if the team uses them; keep client-facing email cleaner. Match the other person's level of formality, never out-casual the founder.

cards.prompt: On chat, it is better to send 'Hi' first and wait for a reply before asking your actual question.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Put the whole question in one message. Making someone wait for the real point wastes their time and yours.
cards.whenWrong: No. The 'hi, then wait' pattern is a known annoyance. Write the full question in one message so they can answer whenever they look.

cards.prompt: Telling a client your working hours and reply rhythm makes you look less professional.
cards.whenRight: Right. The opposite is true. Predictability builds trust; a client who knows your rhythm stops wondering and stops micromanaging.
cards.whenWrong: It actually makes you look more professional. Stating your hours and response time removes uncertainty, and certainty is what calm clients are made of.

items.title: Map the channels for Kola
items.body:
Part 1. For each message, decide the best channel (email, chat, voice note/Loom, or call) and write one sentence on why:
1. Confirming an order shipped, to a customer.
2. Asking Ama a quick yes/no about a deposit, mid-afternoon.
3. Walking a new team member through how to use the order tracker.
4. Telling Ama that a big customer is threatening to cancel a large order.
5. Sending the supplier the finalised purchase order.

Part 2. Write a short "How I work" note you could send a new client, stating your working hours, your reply time, and which channel to use for urgent things. Save both under a new "Channels" heading in your Toolkit.

days.title: Ship your Communication Toolkit
days.summary: Assemble your reusable templates and write three real executive emails. Your first portfolio piece.

items.title: Turn a week of practice into an asset
items.body:
## Why templates make you fast and consistent
You will write the same kinds of messages over and over: a follow-up, a status update, a scheduling note, a polite no, an apology. Re-thinking each one from scratch is slow and inconsistent. A professional keeps a personal template library: a starting point they adapt in seconds. That is what makes an experienced operator look effortless, they are not faster typists, they are not starting from a blank page.

Today you finish that library, and you write three real emails for Ama that go straight into your portfolio. When a future client asks "can you actually write well?", you do not say yes, you show them these.

## What makes a good template
A template is a skeleton with the structure baked in and `[brackets]` for the parts that change:

> **Follow-up template**
> Subject: Following up, [topic] ([what you need])
> Hi [name],
> Following up on [thing], which was due [date]. Could you [specific ask] by [deadline]? If [obstacle], let me know and I will [your backup plan].
> Thanks, [your name]

The structure (specific reference, clear ask, deadline, backup plan) is the value. You adapt the brackets in 20 seconds and send something that reads like you thought hard about it.

## The portfolio standard
Everything you keep this week should pass the stranger test: someone who has never met you reads it and thinks *I would let this person handle my inbox.* Clean formatting, no typos, specific, warm, scannable. This is the bar for every deliverable in this track. A portfolio is not a list of things you learned, it is a set of artefacts that prove you can do the work. You are building the first one today.

cards.prompt: A portfolio is best described as a list of the topics and tools you have studied.
cards.whenRight: Correct. A portfolio is a set of real artefacts that prove you can do the work, not a list of things you learned. Show, do not tell.
cards.whenWrong: Rethink it. Clients do not hire from a syllabus. A portfolio is the actual work, the emails, the toolkit, the projects, that proves you can do the job.

cards.prompt: Keeping a personal template library is what lets experienced operators produce good messages quickly.
cards.whenRight: Yes. They are not faster typists, they start from a proven skeleton and adapt the brackets, so they are fast and consistent at once.
cards.whenWrong: It is. The speed comes from never starting from a blank page. A good template bakes in the structure; you just adapt the variable parts.

items.title: Final build: Toolkit + 3 executive emails
items.body:
This is the Week 1 portfolio deliverable. In your Communication Toolkit doc, complete two things.

**Part A, the Toolkit.** Fill in all five template sections with clean, reusable templates (use `[brackets]` for the variable parts): Status Update, Follow-Up, Scheduling, Saying No, Apology / Bad News. Pull from your practice all week.

**Part B, three executive emails for Ama.** Write three polished, ready-to-send emails as if you are Ama's assistant:
1. An email to a supplier (Kwesi at Northern Weavers) following up on a late order of 50 baskets, originally due last Friday.
2. An email to the whole Kola team announcing that the Monday standup is moving to Tuesdays at 10am GMT, with a one-line reason.
3. A reply to an upset customer whose anniversary gift arrived a week late (you have refunded shipping and the item is now delivered).

Each email must use what you learned: a scannable subject line, BLUF, a clear ask or next step, and a warm-but-competent tone. Proofread every one. Export the finished doc as a PDF named "Communication-Toolkit-YourName.pdf". This is your first portfolio artefact and your Week 1 submission.

topics: What a remote operator does and what they are really paid for
Business writing and BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front)
The three-pass edit (point, cut, action)
Email anatomy: subject lines, structure, tone
cc, bcc, and reply-all etiquette
Managing up: Done/Doing/Blocked status updates
Asking good questions (situation, options, recommendation)
Hard conversations: saying no, apologising, defusing anger
Meeting etiquette: agendas, notes, async vs sync, time zones
Choosing channels (email, chat, voice) and setting response norms
tasks: Create a clean professional email address, signature, and headshot
Start a Communication Toolkit doc with five template sections
Rewrite three rambling messages using BLUF and the three-pass edit
Write five scannable subject lines and one full approval email
Write a Done/Doing/Blocked status update and three well-formed questions
Draft a reply that defuses an angry customer, plus a polite 'no'
Produce a meeting agenda and post-meeting notes with action items
Map message types to channels and write a 'how I work' note
Finish the five-section Toolkit and write three executive emails for Ama
weeks.project: Build your Communication Toolkit: a single document containing five reusable message templates (status update, follow-up, scheduling, saying no, apology/bad news) plus three polished executive emails written on behalf of Ama Mensah, founder of Kola (a late-supplier follow-up, a team scheduling announcement, and an upset-customer reply). Export it as a clean PDF. This is portfolio artefact #1 of 10.
exercises: Rewrite three rambling messages with BLUF, cutting length by a third
Write five specific subject lines and one full budget-approval email
Write a status update and convert three vague questions into good ones
Draft a calm, concrete reply to a genuinely angry customer email
Map five message types to the right channel and justify each
questions: What is a remote operator actually paid for, and why is writing central to it?
What does BLUF mean and when do you use it?
When is bcc appropriate and when is it a reputation risk?
What are the three parts of a strong status update?
What is the structure of a good question that removes work from your boss?
outputs: Communication Toolkit PDF with five reusable templates
Three polished executive emails written for Ama / Kola
Professional email address, signature, and headshot set up
A status update, a defused angry-customer reply, and a channel map
mastery_questions: Set up a professional email address, signature, and profile photo and screenshot the result
Write a BLUF version of a rambling message so the main point is in the first line
Cut a wordy sentence by removing hedges (just, maybe, I think) without losing meaning
Write a scannable subject line that includes the topic and the deadline
Compose a five-part email (greeting, BLUF, body, clear ask with deadline, sign-off) under 120 words
Write a Done/Doing/Blocked status update for a realistic week of work
Turn a vague question into a good one with situation, options, and your recommendation
Write a reply that defuses an angry customer using acknowledge, apologise, act
Write a polite 'no' that acknowledges, declines clearly, and offers an alternative
Produce post-meeting notes listing decisions made and action items as '[owner] will [task] by [date]'
weeks.ai_assist: Use AI as your writing coach, never as the author who replaces your judgement. Three high-value moves this week: (1) Paste a draft email into ChatGPT or Claude and ask "make this clearer and more concise without changing the meaning, and tell me what you cut and why", then learn from the edits. (2) Ask it to role-play a difficult client so you can practise replies. (3) Ask "what is the unstated assumption a busy founder might misread in this message?" Always read and edit AI output before sending. A client can tell when a message is generic AI text, so use AI to sharpen your voice, not to mute it.
weeks.pre_flight: Before you write a single template, look at your own last 10 sent messages (email or WhatsApp). For each, ask: would a stranger know what this is about and what to do, in ten seconds? Count how many pass and write the number down. At the end of the week, rewrite those same ten messages and compare. The gap is the skill you built.
common_mistakes: Burying the ask in the middle of a paragraph so a skimming reader misses it
Over-apologising or over-hedging (just, sorry to bother, no rush, maybe) until you sound junior
Vague subject lines like 'Question' or 'Update' that get deprioritised in a busy inbox
Going silent when a deadline will slip instead of flagging it early with a new date
Hitting reply-all when only one person needed the response
weeks.debug_help: When a message is not landing (no reply, or the wrong reply), do not just resend it louder. Re-read it as the recipient: is the ask obvious and is there a deadline? Is the main point in the first line? Did you ask for too many things at once? Most 'they are ignoring me' problems are really 'my message gave them no clear, single, easy next action' problems. Rewrite it down to one clear ask with a date and it usually moves. If you are stuck on tone, paste it into Claude and ask whether it reads as warm and competent, or cold, or junior, then adjust.
stretch: Write a sixth template: the cold introduction email to a potential new client
Record a 60-second Loom or voice-note version of one update (many founders prefer voice)
Create a one-page 'how I communicate' doc you could send a new client to set expectations

weeks.title: Digital productivity systems
weeks.context:
A remote operator is only as good as their system. Last week you learned to communicate; this week you build the machine that lets you keep ten things straight without dropping any. When you are juggling Ama's inbox, the team's tasks, supplier files, and your own work, memory is not a plan. Memory is how things get lost.

You will build a real digital workspace: a clean file structure in Google Drive, a second brain in Notion, a single place where every task lives, and a daily planning habit. The test is simple, by Friday a stranger should be able to open your workspace and find any file in under ten seconds, and you should never again answer a client with "sorry, I think I lost that".

By the end of the week you will have a workspace you could hand to a client on day one and look like someone who has done this for years.

concept_check.q: Ama asks for 'the September supplier invoice' and you have 400 files in one folder with names like 'invoice', 'invoice (1)', 'scan2'. What is the real problem?
choices: You need a faster computer
You need a folder structure and a naming convention so files are findable
You should delete old files
You should email Ama to ask which invoice she means
concept_check.explain: Findability is a system problem, not a memory or speed problem. A logical folder tree plus a naming convention means you find anything in seconds, even files you never touched.

concept_check.q: You capture tasks in your head, on sticky notes, in WhatsApp to yourself, and in three different apps. What happens?
choices: You stay flexible and fast
Things slip through the cracks because there is no single source of truth
Nothing, as long as you check all of them
It only matters for big tasks
concept_check.explain: Scattered capture guarantees dropped work. The core rule of any productivity system is one trusted place where every task lives, so you only have to look in one spot.

concept_check.q: Which system is better: a beautiful, complex Notion setup with 12 databases, or a simple one you actually update every day?
choices: The complex one, it is more professional
The simple one you actually maintain
They are equal
Neither, use paper
concept_check.explain: A system you abandon is worthless. The best system is the simplest one that prevents lost work and that you will genuinely keep up. Maintainability beats sophistication.

days.title: Why a system beats memory, and set up your tools
days.summary: Understand why operators run on systems, then create your Drive and Notion accounts and the base structure.

items.title: Memory is not a system
items.body:
## The hidden job of an operator
Last week was about the words you send. This week is about the machine behind them. When Ama hands you her operations, she is also handing you the mental load she was carrying: where is that file, did that task get done, when is that deadline. If you carry all of that in your head, you become the bottleneck, and eventually you drop something. The fix is to move the load out of your head and into a system.

## What a 'system' actually means
A productivity system is just three reliable habits with tools behind them:
1. **One place for files** that is organised so anything is findable in seconds.
2. **One place for tasks** so nothing is ever 'kept in mind' (and therefore forgotten).
3. **One daily rhythm** that turns a pile of work into a plan.

That is it. Not twelve apps. The operators who look calm under a heavy load are not superhuman, their system is catching the balls so their brain does not have to.

## Why this is worth a whole week
A client cannot see your effort, but they feel your reliability. "Can you send me the August sales sheet?" answered in fifteen seconds, every time, is what makes Ama trust you with bigger things. "Um, let me look for it..." said twice is what makes her start doing the work herself again. The system is invisible until the moment it saves you, and it saves you constantly.

## This week's destination
You will set up a real Google Drive structure, a Notion second brain with a task board, a naming convention, and a daily planning template, then write a one-page guide so anyone could navigate it. That guide plus the workspace is portfolio artefact number two.

items.title: Set up your workspace foundation, step by step
items.body:
## Do this now
You only need free tools this week. Set up the two that run almost every remote operation.

**1. Google Drive.** You already have a Google account from Week 1, so you have Drive. Go to drive.google.com. Create one top-level folder named for your client, for example `Kola`. Inside it, create these subfolders: `01 Admin`, `02 Finance`, `03 Suppliers`, `04 Customers`, `05 Marketing`, `06 SOPs`. The number prefixes force a sensible order instead of alphabetical chaos. You should now see a clean, numbered list of folders, this is the spine of everything.

**2. Notion.** Go to notion.so and sign up free with your professional email. Create a new page called `Kola HQ`. This will become your second brain: a task board, notes, and links to the Drive folders, all in one place. Do not build anything fancy yet, just create the page. You should see a blank page with a title, that is the starting point for Day 3.

**3. A test file.** Drop any document into `01 Admin` so the structure is not empty. Right-click it and check you can rename and move it. Confirm you can share a folder: right-click `Kola` > Share, and notice the permission options (Viewer, Commenter, Editor). You will use those constantly.

That is the foundation. Everything this week hangs off these two tools.

cards.prompt: Number-prefixing folders (01 Admin, 02 Finance) is pointless because Drive sorts alphabetically anyway.
cards.whenRight: Correct. That is exactly why you prefix them: numbers force the order YOU want instead of alphabetical accident, so the important folders sit where you expect.
cards.whenWrong: The prefix is the point. Alphabetical sorting scatters your folders randomly; '01', '02' pins them in a deliberate, logical order.

cards.prompt: The goal of a productivity system is to have as many specialised apps as possible.
cards.whenRight: Right. More apps means more places to check and more places to lose things. The goal is few, trusted places: one for files, one for tasks, one daily rhythm.
cards.whenWrong: No. App-sprawl is the disease, not the cure. A good system uses few trusted places so you never wonder where something lives.

items.title: Your turn, build the foundation
items.body:
Tick each box only when it is truly done.

- [ ] Created a top-level Drive folder for your client (e.g. `Kola`)
- [ ] Created the six numbered subfolders (Admin, Finance, Suppliers, Customers, Marketing, SOPs)
- [ ] Signed up for Notion (free) with your professional email and created a `Kola HQ` page
- [ ] Dropped a test file into `01 Admin` and confirmed you can rename, move, and share it
- [ ] Checked the three Drive sharing permission levels (Viewer, Commenter, Editor)

Deliverable: a screenshot of your Drive folder structure.

days.title: File organisation and naming conventions
days.summary: A naming convention turns a pile of files into a searchable database.

items.title: Name files so future-you can find them
items.body:
## The problem with 'invoice (3)'
Default file names are written for the moment you save them and useless a week later. `scan2.pdf`, `invoice.pdf`, `final_FINAL_v2.docx`, none of these tell you what is inside without opening it. Multiply by 400 files and you have a swamp.

## A naming convention
A convention is just an agreed pattern for naming every file. A reliable one for operations work:

`YYYY-MM-DD_Category_Description_vN`

Examples:
- `2026-09-03_Invoice_NorthernWeavers_baskets.pdf`
- `2026-09-01_Report_AugustSales.xlsx`
- `2026-08-28_Contract_AmaSignature_v2.pdf`

Why it works: the date-first format sorts chronologically on its own, the category groups similar files, the description tells you the contents at a glance, and the version number kills the 'final_FINAL' problem. You can now find any file by sorting by name or searching one keyword.

## Pick one and never deviate
The power is in consistency. A perfect convention you follow half the time is worse than a simple one you follow every time. Decide your pattern, write it at the top of your `06 SOPs` folder, and apply it to every new file from now on. When you join a client who already has a convention, use theirs, do not impose yours.

## A word on folders vs search
Good names make folders less critical, because you can search. But folders still matter for sharing (you share a folder, not 50 files) and for the mental map. Aim for shallow folders (two or three levels deep at most); deeply nested folders are where files go to die.

cards.prompt: Starting file names with the date in YYYY-MM-DD format makes them sort in chronological order automatically.
cards.whenRight: Yes. YYYY-MM-DD sorts correctly as text, so a name-sort becomes a date-sort for free. That is why date-first naming is so common in operations.
cards.whenWrong: It does work. Because YYYY-MM-DD sorts the same as text and as dates, putting it first makes your files line up chronologically with no effort.

cards.prompt: A simple naming convention you follow every time beats a perfect one you follow half the time.
cards.whenRight: Right. Consistency is the whole value. A pattern with gaps is unreliable, and an unreliable system is one you stop trusting.
cards.whenWrong: Consistency wins. The benefit comes from EVERY file matching the pattern; a half-followed convention leaves you guessing again.

items.title: Design and apply a convention
items.body:
1. Write your file naming convention in one line, with the pattern and what each part means.
2. Give five example file names that follow it (an invoice, a report, a contract, a product photo, a meeting note).
3. Take five badly-named sample files (make them up: 'doc1', 'IMG_4432', 'final', 'new sheet', 'untitled') and rename each to your convention.
4. Save the convention as a note in your `06 SOPs` folder so it is documented for any future teammate.

Deliverable: the convention line plus before/after names for the five files.

days.title: Google Workspace and sharing without leaks
days.summary: Docs, Sheets, and Drive sharing done right, including the permission mistakes that embarrass people.

items.title: Drive, Docs, Sheets, and safe sharing
items.body:
## The three tools you will live in
Most remote operations run on Google Workspace because it is free, collaborative, and everyone has it.
- **Docs** for anything written: SOPs, meeting notes, drafts, plans. Real-time collaboration means Ama can comment without emailing a new version back and forth.
- **Sheets** for anything with rows: order trackers, budgets, content calendars, contact lists. You do not need to be an Excel wizard; basic formulas (SUM, simple filtering, sorting) cover most operations work.
- **Drive** to hold it all, organised with your folders and convention.

## Sharing: the part people get wrong
Sharing is where careless operators leak data or block access. The rules:
- **Share folders, not individual files**, where possible, so new files inside are covered automatically.
- **Pick the right permission**: Viewer (can read), Commenter (can suggest, cannot change), Editor (can change everything). Default to the least access that lets the person do their job. A supplier needs Viewer on a purchase order, not Editor.
- **Be careful with 'Anyone with the link'.** It is convenient and dangerous, anyone who ever gets that link can see the file forever. For sensitive things (finance, contracts), share with specific email addresses only.
- **Check before you send.** Before sharing a link with a client, open it in an incognito window to confirm it actually works and shows what you intend. The 'you need access' reply is a small but avoidable credibility hit.

## A reliability habit
When you create something a client will need, share it proactively and say so: "I have put the August report in the Finance folder and shared it with you, link here." They never have to ask where things are. That is the feeling you are selling.

cards.prompt: Giving a supplier 'Editor' access to your purchase order is the safe default.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Default to the least access needed. A supplier should usually get Viewer; Editor lets them change the document, which you rarely want.
cards.whenWrong: Too much access. The safe default is the minimum that lets them do the job. For reading a PO, that is Viewer, not Editor.

cards.prompt: Opening a share link in an incognito window before sending it is a smart way to confirm it works.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Incognito shows what an outsider sees, so you catch 'you need access' errors before the client does.
cards.whenWrong: It is smart. Incognito simulates someone who is not logged in as you, which is the fastest way to verify a link actually works for the recipient.

items.title: Build a tracker and share it safely
items.body:
1. In Google Sheets, build a simple order tracker for Kola with columns: Order ID, Customer, Item, Date, Status, Amount.
2. Add five sample rows and a SUM of the Amount column.
3. Save it into your `04 Customers` folder using your naming convention.
4. Share it with one test address as Commenter, then open the link in an incognito window to confirm it works and shows the right access.

Deliverable: a screenshot of the tracker plus a note of which permission you used and why.

days.title: Notion as a second brain
days.summary: Turn the blank Notion page into a real operations hub: tasks, notes, and links in one place.

items.title: Build your operations hub in Notion
items.body:
## Why Notion
Drive holds your files. Notion holds everything else: your tasks, your notes, your client information, your links, your SOPs index, all on pages you can shape however you want. Think of it as the front desk of your operation, the one page you open first every morning.

## The minimum viable hub
Do not build a cathedral. On your `Kola HQ` page, add four sections (type `/` in Notion to insert blocks):
1. **A task board.** Add a Board database (type `/board`). It gives you columns To Do, In Progress, Done. Each card is a task you drag across as it moves. This is your single source of truth for work.
2. **Quick notes.** A simple text area for things you need to remember: passwords location, Ama's preferences, recurring questions.
3. **Key links.** Links to the Drive folders, the order tracker, the website admin, so you never hunt for them.
4. **People.** A short list of who is who: Ama, the team, key suppliers, key customers, with one line each.

## The discipline that makes it work
A second brain only works if you actually put things in it. Build the habit: the moment a task appears (an email, a request, a thought in the shower), it goes on the board, not in your head. The moment you learn something about the client (Ama prefers voice notes, the courier is closed Sundays), it goes in quick notes. Capture first, organise later. An empty, tidy Notion is useless; a slightly messy one you actually use is gold.

## Notion vs Drive vs Sheets, when to use which
Rough rule: structured rows of data go in Sheets, long written documents go in Docs/Drive, and your day-to-day operating hub (tasks, notes, links) goes in Notion. Notion can do databases too, so some people run trackers there as well, either is fine. Pick what you will maintain.

cards.prompt: A second brain works best when you capture tasks and notes into it the moment they appear, not later.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Capture-first is the whole point: if it goes into the system immediately, it cannot be forgotten. Sorting can happen later.
cards.whenWrong: Capture-first is the key habit. If you wait to log things 'later', later often never comes and the task is lost.

cards.prompt: You should build the most elaborate Notion setup possible before you start using it.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Start minimal and grow it as real needs appear. An over-built system you do not maintain is worse than a simple one you use daily.
cards.whenWrong: No. Elaborate-before-use is how systems get abandoned. Build the minimum hub, use it, and add only what you actually need.

items.title: Build the Kola HQ hub
items.body:
On your `Kola HQ` Notion page, build the four sections:
- [ ] A Board database (To Do / In Progress / Done) with at least five real-looking tasks
- [ ] A Quick Notes section with three things to remember about the client
- [ ] A Key Links section linking to your Drive folders and order tracker
- [ ] A People section listing Ama, one teammate, and one supplier with a one-line note each

Deliverable: a screenshot (or share link) of your Kola HQ page.

days.title: One place for every task
days.summary: A capture system so nothing is ever 'kept in mind' and then forgotten.

items.title: Capture everything, decide later
items.body:
## The cost of 'I will remember that'
Every task you hold in your head is a small, constant drain, and eventually one slips. Ama mentions in passing that the courier needs a new address; you are mid-task; you tell yourself you will do it later; you forget; a parcel goes to the wrong place. That is not carelessness, it is a system gap. The fix is total capture: every task, request, and idea goes into one trusted place the instant it appears.

## How capture works in practice
1. **One inbox for tasks.** Your Notion board's To Do column (or a Sheet, or a simple list) is the only place tasks live. Email requests, WhatsApp asks, your own ideas, all land here.
2. **Make capture frictionless.** It has to take five seconds or you will not do it. Keep Notion open in a pinned tab; on your phone, use the Notion app or even a quick note you sweep into the board daily.
3. **A task is a clear action.** Write 'Email courier the new pickup address by Thu' not 'courier'. A vague task is one you will avoid because you have to re-think it every time you see it.

## Process, do not just collect
Capture without processing becomes a graveyard. Once a day, run your task list: for each item, do it now if it takes under two minutes, schedule it if it is bigger, delegate it if it is not yours, or delete it if it no longer matters. This quick daily pass keeps the list trustworthy, and a trustworthy list is one your brain can finally let go of.

## The payoff
When everything is captured and processed, you can honestly tell a client "it is on my list and it will be done by Thursday" and mean it. That sentence, reliably true, is worth more than any single piece of work.

cards.prompt: A task written as 'courier' is just as useful as 'Email courier the new pickup address by Thursday'.
cards.whenRight: Correct. A vague task makes you re-think it every time, so you avoid it. A clear action with a deadline is one you can just do.
cards.whenWrong: Not equal. 'Courier' forces you to reconstruct what you meant. A specific action plus a deadline is what actually gets done.

cards.prompt: If a captured task takes under two minutes, the efficient move is usually to just do it now.
cards.whenRight: Yes. The two-minute rule: tiny tasks cost more to track than to do, so clear them immediately during your daily pass.
cards.whenWrong: Doing it now is usually right. Tracking a 30-second task across days costs more attention than just finishing it on the spot.

items.title: Run a capture and process pass
items.body:
1. Brain-dump every task, real or imagined, for running Kola for a week into your task board's To Do column (aim for 12 to 15).
2. Rewrite any vague ones as clear actions with a verb and, where it matters, a deadline.
3. Process the list: mark which you would do now (under two minutes), schedule, delegate, or delete.

Deliverable: your processed task list with each item labelled do-now / schedule / delegate / delete.

days.title: Time management and the daily plan
days.summary: Time-blocking turns a long task list into a realistic day.

items.title: Plan the day, not just the list
items.body:
## A list is not a plan
A task list tells you what to do. It does not tell you when, and it has no sense of how many hours you actually have. That is why long lists feel overwhelming and half-finished: you keep starting whatever is loudest and run out of day. A plan assigns tasks to time.

## Time-blocking
Time-blocking means giving each chunk of work a slot on your calendar. Instead of a floating list of ten things, your day looks like:
- 09:00 to 09:30, process inbox and reply to anything under five minutes
- 09:30 to 10:30, ship yesterday's orders and update the tracker
- 10:30 to 11:00, supplier follow-ups
- 11:00 to 12:00, build the content calendar (focus block, no chat)

Two things happen. First, you confront reality, you cannot block twelve hours of work into a six-hour day, so you prioritise honestly. Second, you defend focus, a labelled block is a promise to yourself that this hour is for this one thing.

## The daily plan ritual
Spend the first ten minutes of each day (or the last ten of the day before) turning your task list into a blocked plan. Pick the two or three things that matter most and block them first, ideally in your sharpest hours. Leave buffer, things overrun and urgent issues land, so a day packed to the minute always breaks. Aim to plan about 70% of your time and leave the rest for the unexpected.

## Match energy to task
Do demanding, brain-heavy work (writing a report, planning) when you are freshest. Save shallow work (filing, simple replies) for low-energy stretches. An operator who schedules the hard thing for their best hour gets more done than one who grinds randomly all day.

cards.prompt: Blocking your entire day minute-to-minute with no buffer is the most productive approach.
cards.whenRight: Correct. No buffer means the first overrun or urgent issue breaks the whole plan. Plan about 70% and leave room for reality.
cards.whenWrong: Over-packing backfires. Tasks run long and surprises happen; a plan with no buffer collapses by mid-morning. Leave slack.

cards.prompt: It is smart to schedule your hardest, most focus-heavy task for your sharpest hours.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Match energy to task: deep work in your best hours, shallow work when you are tired. You get far more from the same day.
cards.whenWrong: It is smart. Your best hours are scarce; spending them on demanding work (and leaving filing for tired hours) maximises output.

items.title: Build a time-blocked day
items.body:
1. Take your processed task list from Day 4.
2. Build a time-blocked plan for one realistic working day (use your real available hours), assigning each major task a slot.
3. Put your two most important tasks in your sharpest hours, and leave at least 30% of the day as buffer.
4. Save this as a reusable `Daily Plan` template in Notion or Docs.

Deliverable: your blocked day plus the blank reusable template.

days.title: Information management and the weekly review
days.summary: Keep the system clean so it stays trustworthy, with one habit: the weekly review.

items.title: The weekly review keeps the system alive
items.body:
## Systems decay without maintenance
Any system drifts. Files land in the wrong folder, tasks pile up half-done, notes go stale. Left alone for a month, even a good setup becomes a mess you no longer trust, and a system you do not trust is one you abandon. The cure is a small, regular maintenance habit: the weekly review.

## The weekly review, in 20 minutes
Once a week (Friday afternoon works well), run a short loop:
1. **Clear the task inbox.** Process anything that got captured but not sorted.
2. **Review the board.** Move done tasks to Done, re-date anything that slipped, delete what no longer matters.
3. **Tidy files.** Move any stray files into the right folders, fix any names that broke the convention.
4. **Look ahead.** Glance at next week, what deadlines, meetings, or deliverables are coming? Block the big ones now.
5. **Write the client update.** A weekly Done/Doing/Blocked (from Week 1) falls out of this review naturally, you have just looked at everything.

## Information management
Beyond tasks and files, you accumulate knowledge about the client: how Ama likes things, supplier quirks, recurring customer questions. Capture this somewhere durable (your Notion notes, or a 'client playbook' doc) instead of in your memory. When you eventually hand work to someone else, or come back after a break, that captured knowledge is what lets the operation run without you holding it all in your head.

## The compounding effect
Twenty minutes a week keeps the whole system trustworthy, which means every other day runs faster. Skip it for a month and you spend a painful afternoon digging out. The review is the cheapest insurance you will buy.

cards.prompt: A productivity system, once set up, stays organised on its own.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Every system drifts. Without a small regular review, files scatter and tasks rot until you stop trusting it.
cards.whenWrong: It does not. Systems decay; a weekly review is the maintenance that keeps yours trustworthy enough to actually rely on.

cards.prompt: A weekly review naturally produces the material for your weekly client status update.
cards.whenRight: Yes. By the end of the review you have looked at everything done, in progress, and blocked, which is exactly the update.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Since the review surveys all your work, the Done/Doing/Blocked update writes itself from what you just saw.

items.title: Write and run a weekly review checklist
items.body:
1. Write a weekly review checklist (the five steps, adapted to your setup) and save it in `06 SOPs`.
2. Actually run it on your current workspace: clear the task inbox, tidy the board, fix any file names, and note next week's deadlines.
3. From the review, draft a one-paragraph Done/Doing/Blocked update for Ama.

Deliverable: the checklist plus the status update it produced.

days.title: Ship your digital workspace
days.summary: Package the workspace and write the one-page guide. Portfolio artefact #2.

items.title: Make the workspace handover-ready
items.body:
## A workspace is only done when someone else can use it
You have built a Drive structure, a naming convention, a Notion hub, a capture system, a daily plan, and a weekly review. The final step turns it from 'your setup' into a professional asset: documentation. A workspace a client can understand without you standing over their shoulder is what separates an operator from a freelancer who keeps everything in their own head.

## The one-page workspace guide
Write a single page that explains your system to a newcomer:
- Where files live (the folder structure and what each folder is for)
- The naming convention, with examples
- Where tasks live and how the board works
- The daily plan and weekly review rhythm
- Key links

Keep it short and plain. The test: could Ama, or a future second assistant, read this page and navigate everything without asking you a single question?

## Why this is portfolio gold
When you pitch a future client, 'I will organise your operations' is a claim. This workspace plus its guide is proof. It shows you do not just do tasks, you build systems that make a business run smoother, and that is a far more valuable, far better-paid thing to be.

cards.prompt: A workspace counts as finished once it works for you, even if no one else could navigate it.
cards.whenRight: Correct. The professional standard is handover-ready: documented so a client or future teammate can use it without you. That is what makes it an asset.
cards.whenWrong: Not finished. A system only you understand keeps you as the bottleneck. Documentation is what turns it into something a business can rely on.

cards.prompt: Documenting your system makes you more valuable, not more replaceable.
cards.whenRight: Yes. It proves you build systems, not just do tasks, which is the higher-paid skill. It also frees you to take on more.
cards.whenWrong: More valuable. Operators who build documented systems get trusted with bigger responsibilities; the ones who hoard knowledge stay stuck doing the same tasks.

items.title: Final build: workspace + one-page guide
items.body:

**Part A.** Make sure your workspace is complete and tidy: Drive folders with the convention applied, the Notion hub with a real task board, your daily plan template, and your weekly review checklist.

**Part B.** Write the one-page Workspace Guide covering file locations, the naming convention, the task system, the daily/weekly rhythm, and key links. Make it readable by a total newcomer.

Export the guide as a PDF named `Workspace-Guide-YourName.pdf` and keep the workspace shareable. This is portfolio artefact #2.

weeks.title: Email and calendar management
weeks.context:
This is the bread and butter of executive support, and the skill most clients hire for first. A founder's inbox is where their day gets hijacked. If you can take it over and make it calm, you have made yourself indispensable. This week you learn to take a chaotic inbox to zero, build filters and labels that triage automatically, manage a calendar across time zones, and coordinate meetings without the endless back-and-forth.

You will run a mock CEO inbox and calendar for Ama: 40 messy emails, five meetings to book (one international), a double-booking to untangle, and a supplier trip to plan. By Friday the chaos is a system, and you have documented it so it runs the same way every week.

Master this week and you can walk into almost any remote role tomorrow, because every founder on earth is drowning in email and looking for someone to fix it.

concept_check.q: Ama gets 80 emails a day. What is the most sustainable way to keep her inbox calm?
choices: Read and reply to every email the moment it arrives
Set up filters and labels so routine mail is sorted automatically, and only real decisions reach the main view
Archive everything older than a week
Turn off email notifications and check once a day
concept_check.explain: The goal is fewer items needing a human, not faster human sorting. Automation (filters, labels) handles the routine so only genuine decisions land in front of you or the founder.

concept_check.q: You book a call with a client in London for '3pm'. You are in Accra. What is the risk?
choices: None, 3pm is 3pm everywhere
Accra and London can be the same or an hour apart depending on the season, and without stating the zone someone shows up at the wrong time
The client will be offended by the short notice
Calendar apps cannot handle time zones
concept_check.explain: Always state the zone (e.g. '3pm GMT'). Ambiguous times cause missed international calls, one of the most avoidable and damaging early mistakes.

concept_check.q: What is 'inbox zero'?
choices: Having literally no emails in your account
A state where every email has been processed into an action, a label, or the archive, so nothing is left undecided
Deleting all emails at the end of each day
Replying to every email within five minutes
concept_check.explain: Inbox zero is about decisions, not deletion. Every message has been triaged (do, defer, delegate, file, or delete) so nothing sits unread and undecided.

days.title: The inbox-zero mindset, and set up your triage system
days.summary: Understand what inbox zero really means, then set up Gmail labels and filters that do the sorting for you.

items.title: Inbox zero is about decisions, not deletion
items.body:
## Why the inbox runs the founder's day
An unmanaged inbox is a to-do list other people write for you. Every unread email is a small open loop, and a founder with 200 of them feels permanently behind. When you take over Ama's inbox, you are not just 'answering email', you are giving her back her attention. That is why this is the single most-hired-for skill in remote operations.

## What inbox zero actually means
Inbox zero does not mean an empty account or deleting everything. It means **every email has been processed into a decision**, so nothing sits unread and undecided. For each message there are five possible moves (some people call it the 5 Ds):
- **Do** it now if it takes under two minutes.
- **Defer** it: it needs real work, so it becomes a task with a date.
- **Delegate** it: it is not yours, forward it to who owns it.
- **File** it: no action needed, label and archive it for reference.
- **Delete** it: junk.

After this pass, the inbox view is empty not because mail vanished, but because every item has a home. That is the calm you are selling.

## The mindset shift
Amateurs treat the inbox as a place to live in all day. Pros treat it as a queue they process in dedicated blocks (say, twice a day) and otherwise leave closed. Constant inbox-checking shatters focus; scheduled processing keeps it calm and gets more done. You will set Ama up this way.

items.title: 7 Proven Gmail Tips to Reach Inbox Zero (and stay there!)
items.creator: Simpletivity
items.why: Scott from Simpletivity is a respected productivity teacher. This shows the exact Gmail moves (labels, filters, archive) you will set up below. Watch it, then build the system on your own inbox in the exercise.

items.title: Set up labels and filters, step by step
items.body:
## Do this in your own Gmail now
You will practise on your own inbox so the muscle memory is real.

**1. Create labels (your triage categories).** In Gmail, scroll the left sidebar to 'More' > 'Create new label'. Make four: `Action` (needs you to do something), `Waiting` (you replied, waiting on someone), `Reference` (keep, no action), and `Receipts`. Labels are how you find things after archiving.

**2. Create a filter that auto-sorts.** Click the search bar's filter icon (sliders), or Settings > Filters and Blocked Addresses > Create a new filter. Try: from `noreply@` or anything with 'unsubscribe', then 'Create filter' > 'Skip the Inbox (Archive it)' + 'Apply label: Reference'. Now newsletters never clutter the main view again, they are quietly filed.

**3. Test it.** Send yourself (or find) a newsletter and confirm it lands under the label, not the inbox. That is the result you want: routine mail sorting itself.

**4. Archive vs delete.** Archive (the box icon) removes mail from the inbox but keeps it, searchable forever. Delete is for true junk. When in doubt, archive, storage is cheap and a deleted client email is a problem.

Repeat this for two or three common sender types and your inbox already does a third of the work itself.

cards.prompt: Archiving an email deletes it permanently.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Archive removes it from the inbox but keeps it fully searchable. Delete is the permanent one, reserve it for true junk.
cards.whenWrong: No. Archive just files the email out of the inbox; you can always find it by search or label. Delete is the permanent action.

cards.prompt: A good filter can automatically label and archive routine mail before it ever clutters the inbox.
cards.whenRight: Yes. That is the whole point of filters: routine mail (newsletters, receipts) sorts itself, so only real decisions reach the main view.
cards.whenWrong: It can. Filters auto-apply labels and skip the inbox, so newsletters and receipts file themselves and never add to the founder's load.

items.title: Your turn, build a triage system
items.body:
Set this up on your own Gmail.

- [ ] Created four labels: Action, Waiting, Reference, Receipts
- [ ] Created at least two filters that auto-archive and label routine mail (newsletters, receipts)
- [ ] Tested a filter by confirming a matching email lands under its label, not the inbox
- [ ] Processed 10 real emails using the 5 Ds (do / defer / delegate / file / delete)
