weeks.title: Customer support operations
weeks.context:
Customer support is where many remote operators earn their first international paycheck, and where Kola keeps the customers it worked so hard to win. Every business with customers needs someone calm, clear, and quick to handle questions, complaints, and the occasional angry message. Done well, support is not a cost; it is how a one-time buyer becomes a loyal one.

This week you learn to run support like a pro: a help desk, a reply formula, a library of response macros, the basics of CRMs, and de-escalation that turns an angry customer into a fan. You will run a 15-ticket support simulation for Kola and build the response library that makes good support fast and consistent.

The core truth of support: people remember how you made them feel far longer than they remember the problem. Handle the feeling first, and the rest gets easy.

concept_check.q: A customer messages, clearly upset, that their order is damaged. What should your reply do FIRST?
choices: Explain the return policy and the conditions for a refund
Acknowledge their frustration and that a damaged order is not okay, before getting to the fix
Ask them to send five photos from different angles
Tell them these things happen sometimes
concept_check.explain: Handle the feeling first. People need to feel heard before they can hear a solution. Lead with acknowledgement, then move to the concrete fix.

concept_check.q: You notice 40% of tickets are 'where is my order?'. What is the smartest long-term move?
choices: Reply to each one faster
Reduce the cause: add tracking info to the order confirmation and an FAQ, so fewer customers need to ask
Ignore them; they are easy
Tell customers to be patient
concept_check.explain: Great support does not just answer tickets fast; it removes the reasons tickets happen. A recurring question is a signal to fix something upstream.

concept_check.q: When is a saved response (macro) the right tool, and when is it wrong?
choices: Always use macros; never write custom replies
Use a macro as a starting point for common questions, but always personalise it; never send a generic macro to an emotional or unusual situation
Never use macros; always type everything fresh
Macros are only for spam
concept_check.explain: Macros make routine replies fast and consistent, but they must be personalised, and an angry or unusual situation needs a human, tailored response, not a template.

days.title: The support mindset, and set up your help desk
days.summary: Understand what great support really is, then set up a simple system to handle tickets.

items.title: Support is how you keep customers
items.body:
## The real job of support
Winning a customer is expensive; keeping one is cheap, and support is where you keep them. A customer with a problem is at a fork: handle it well and they often become more loyal than if nothing had gone wrong; handle it badly and they leave and tell others. Support is not damage control, it is one of the highest-leverage things a small business does.

## The mindset
- **The customer is a person, not a ticket.** Behind every message is someone who paid money and wants to feel taken care of.
- **Feeling first, fix second.** People remember how you made them feel. Acknowledge before you solve.
- **You represent the brand.** To the customer, you ARE Kola. Calm, warm, and competent is the brand they should feel.
- **Every ticket is information.** Patterns in tickets tell the business what to fix.

## What you will run
For a small business, support usually flows through email (or a shared inbox), social DMs, and maybe a chat widget. You do not need expensive software to be excellent; you need a system: somewhere tickets land, a way to track them, fast and consistent replies, and a record of each customer.

## This week's destination
You will work a 15-ticket queue for Kola, build a 10+ macro response library, log customers in a simple CRM, and write a report on what you handled and what would reduce future tickets. That package is portfolio artefact number seven, and 'I can run your customer support' is a service you can sell on its own from day one.

items.title: 7 Phrases Customer Service Agents with Astute De-escalation Skills Use Everyday
items.creator: Myra Golden
items.why: Myra Golden trains support teams at major companies. These exact phrases for staying calm and defusing tension are what you will use on the hardest tickets this week. Watch, then practise them on the de-escalation exercise.

items.title: Set up a simple help desk, step by step
items.body:
## You do not need fancy software
Dedicated help desks (Zendesk, Freshscout, Help Scout) are great at scale, and worth knowing by name, but a small business can run excellent support from a shared inbox plus a simple tracker. Set that up now.

**1. A shared support inbox.** A dedicated address like `support@` (or a label in Gmail) so all customer messages land in one place, separate from the founder's personal mail. Everyone who handles support sees the same queue.

**2. A status system.** Use labels or columns to track each ticket's state: `New`, `In Progress`, `Waiting on Customer`, `Resolved`. Now nothing falls through the cracks and you can see the queue at a glance, this is the support version of inbox triage from Week 3.

**3. A simple CRM / customer log.** A Google Sheet with one row per customer: name, contact, order history, and notes from past interactions. When a customer writes in, you can see who they are and what happened before, which lets you treat them like a known person, not a stranger.

**4. Saved responses on.** Enable Gmail Templates (from Week 3) so your macros are ready.

## The flow
A ticket arrives, you label it New, read it, reply (often from a personalised macro), update its status, and log the interaction in the CRM. Resolved tickets get marked Resolved. That loop, run consistently, is professional support.

cards.prompt: Handling a customer's problem well can make them more loyal than if nothing had gone wrong.
cards.whenRight: Yes. A well-handled problem proves the business cares, which often builds more loyalty than a smooth experience that was never tested.
cards.whenWrong: It is true. Recovery done well is powerful: customers remember that you took care of them when it mattered, and many become more loyal for it.

cards.prompt: You need expensive help-desk software to run professional customer support.
cards.whenRight: Correct. A shared inbox, a status system, a simple CRM sheet, and saved responses are enough to run excellent support for a small business.
cards.whenWrong: You do not. Great support is a system, not a tool. A shared inbox plus a tracker and a customer log handles small-business support well.

items.title: Your turn, set up support
items.body:
- [ ] Set up a support inbox or label and four status labels (New, In Progress, Waiting, Resolved)
- [ ] Build a simple CRM sheet (name, contact, order history, notes) with three sample customers
- [ ] Enable saved responses (Gmail Templates)
- [ ] Process two sample tickets through the full loop (read, reply, update status, log)

Deliverable: a screenshot of your status labels and CRM sheet.

days.title: Handling tickets: the reply formula
days.summary: A reliable shape for support replies that works on almost any ticket.

items.title: The support reply formula
items.body:
## One shape, most tickets
Most support replies follow the same shape. Internalise it and you handle any ticket calmly:
1. **Acknowledge.** Show you read and understood, especially the feeling. "Thanks for reaching out, and sorry your order hasn't arrived yet, I completely understand the worry."
2. **Answer or act.** The concrete substance: the answer, or what you are doing. "I've checked and your parcel is in Tema, out for delivery tomorrow."
3. **Next step / set expectation.** What happens now and by when. "I'll personally confirm once it's delivered. If it's not with you by Friday, reply here and I'll escalate immediately."
4. **Warm close.** "Thanks for your patience, and sorry again for the wait."

## Match the energy, do not mirror it
If the customer is calm, be efficient and friendly. If they are upset, slow down and lead with more acknowledgement. Never mirror their anger, your calm is what brings the temperature down. A measured, warm reply to a furious message is disarming.

## Be specific, not corporate
"Your inquiry is important to us and will be processed" says nothing and feels cold. "I've refunded your shipping (you'll see it in 3 to 5 days) and flagged your account so this doesn't happen again" is specific and reassuring. Specifics prove you actually did something.

## Know your authority before you reply
Decide in advance (or confirm with the founder) what you can offer: refunds up to what amount, replacements, discounts, exceptions. Knowing your limits lets you resolve confidently instead of saying 'let me check' to everything. Anything beyond your authority goes to the founder, fast, with your recommendation.

cards.prompt: If a customer's message is angry, matching their tone shows you take them seriously.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Never mirror anger. Your calm, warm reply is what lowers the temperature; matching it escalates.
cards.whenWrong: Mirroring anger makes it worse. Stay calm and warm, that steadiness is what defuses the situation. Match a calm customer's efficiency, not an angry one's heat.

cards.prompt: Knowing in advance what you are allowed to offer (refunds, replacements) lets you resolve tickets confidently.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Clear authority means you act decisively instead of 'let me check' on everything. Anything beyond your limit goes to the founder fast.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Pre-agreed authority is what lets you resolve on the spot. Without it you stall on every ticket; with it you are fast and confident.

items.title: Reply to five tickets
items.body:
Write replies to five varied tickets using the formula (acknowledge, answer/act, next step, warm close):
1. 'Where is my order? It's been a week.'
2. 'Do you ship to the UK and how much?'
3. 'The basket I received is smaller than it looked online.'
4. 'Can I change the delivery address? I just ordered.'
5. 'Your website wouldn't take my payment.'

Decide a sensible support policy for each. Deliverable: the five replies.

days.title: Building a response library
days.summary: Macros that make you fast without making you robotic.

items.title: A macro library for support
items.body:
## Why macros matter even more in support
Support is high-volume and repetitive: the same dozen questions, over and over. Without saved responses you re-type the same answer all day, slowly and inconsistently. A macro library (saved replies) lets you answer the common 80% in seconds and spend your real time on the hard 20%.

## What to build
Cover your most common tickets. For Kola:
- Order status / tracking
- Shipping options and costs
- Returns and refunds
- Out of stock / restock
- Damaged or wrong item
- Address change
- Payment issue
- A warm thank-you for a first order
- A holding reply ('looking into this, will update you by X')
- A de-escalation opener for upset customers

## The golden rule: personalise
A macro is a skeleton, never a finished message. Always fill in the human parts: the customer's name, their actual order number, the specific detail. The customer should never be able to tell it started as a template. Compare 'Dear Customer, your issue is noted' with 'Hi Fatou, I've sorted your refund for order KOLA-318, you'll see it in a few days'. Same speed, completely different feeling.

## A consistent voice
Your macros define Kola's support voice, warm, clear, human. Writing them once and reusing them means every customer gets the same good experience, no matter how busy you are or who is on shift. That consistency is part of what makes support feel professional rather than improvised.

cards.prompt: A macro should be sent exactly as saved so support stays fast and consistent.
cards.whenRight: Correct. A macro is a starting point; always personalise the name, order number, and specifics. Sent verbatim it feels cold and robotic.
cards.whenWrong: Never send it verbatim. The macro saves the structure; you fill in the human details so the customer feels seen, not processed.

cards.prompt: A 'holding reply' that acknowledges the customer and promises an update by a time is a valuable macro.
cards.whenRight: Yes. It buys you time while keeping the customer calm, far better than silence while you work out the answer.
cards.whenWrong: It is valuable. A quick honest holding reply stops the 'are they ignoring me?' spiral and keeps the customer patient while you sort the real fix.

items.title: Build a 10-macro library
items.body:
Write at least 10 reusable support macros for Kola covering the common ticket types listed in the lesson.
For two of them, show the bare macro and a personalised send (with a name and order number).

Deliverable: the 10+ macros plus the two personalised examples.

days.title: CRM basics and customer records
days.summary: Treat every customer like someone you know, because you have the record.

items.title: Remembering the customer
items.body:
## What a CRM is, simply
A CRM (customer relationship management) is just an organised record of your customers and your interactions with them. It can be a dedicated tool (HubSpot, a Shopify customer list) or, for a small business, a well-kept spreadsheet. The point is the same: when a customer contacts you, you can see who they are and what has happened before.

## Why it changes the experience
Without a record, every contact starts from zero, the customer re-explains, you guess. With a record, you open their row and see: this is Fatou, a repeat buyer, her last order had a shipping issue we fixed, she prefers WhatsApp. Now you can say 'Hi Fatou, good to hear from you again' and handle her as a valued, known customer. That small thing builds enormous loyalty.

## What to capture
One row per customer: name, contact (and preferred channel), order history, past issues and how they were resolved, and any notes (preferences, VIP status, anything personal they mentioned). Update it after every meaningful interaction, capture-first, like Week 2.

## Use it proactively
A good record is not just reactive. It lets you spot a VIP and treat them specially, notice a customer who had a bad experience and check in, or see that someone has not ordered in a while. Support shades into retention here: the record is what lets you turn one-time buyers into regulars.

## Privacy matters
Customer data is sensitive. Keep it secure (proper sharing permissions, from Week 2), only collect what you need, and never expose it. Handling customer information carefully is part of being trusted with a business's operations.

cards.prompt: For a small business, a well-kept spreadsheet can serve as a CRM.
cards.whenRight: Yes. A CRM is just an organised record of customers and interactions; a clean sheet does that fine until the business outgrows it.
cards.whenWrong: It can. You do not need expensive software at small scale; a structured sheet (one row per customer, with history and notes) is a real CRM.

cards.prompt: Logging past interactions lets you treat a returning customer as a known person, which builds loyalty.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Seeing their history means you greet them by name and handle them in context, which feels personal and earns loyalty.
cards.whenWrong: It does. A record turns a stranger into a known customer; 'good to hear from you again, Fatou' is only possible if you logged the history.

items.title: Build and use a CRM
items.body:
1. Build a customer log sheet with columns: Name, Contact, Preferred channel, Order history, Past issues/resolutions, Notes.
2. Add five sample customers, including one repeat buyer with a past resolved issue and one VIP.
3. Write the opening line of a reply to the repeat buyer that shows you know their history.

Deliverable: the CRM sheet plus the personalised opening line.

days.title: Conflict resolution and de-escalation
days.summary: Turn a furious customer into a calm, and often loyal, one.

items.title: Defusing the hard ones
items.body:
## The angry customer is an opportunity
Most businesses handle angry customers badly, defensive, slow, robotic, which is exactly why handling them well stands out. A furious customer who is treated with calm respect and a real fix often becomes one of your most loyal, because you exceeded the low bar they expected.

## The de-escalation sequence
1. **Acknowledge and validate the feeling.** "You're absolutely right to be frustrated, this isn't the experience we want for you, and I'm sorry." This single step releases most of the heat. People escalate when they feel unheard.
2. **Take ownership, do not deflect.** No 'the courier did it' or 'our policy says'. "Let me sort this out for you." You can acknowledge a bad experience without admitting legal fault.
3. **Act concretely.** Tell them exactly what you are doing, now. Vague reassurance does not calm anyone; a specific action does.
4. **Follow through and follow up.** Do what you said, then confirm it is done. The follow-up ('just confirming your refund went through') turns a save into loyalty.

## Phrases that work (and ones that do not)
Helpful: 'You're right.' 'I'm sorry this happened.' 'Here's what I'm going to do.' 'Let me make this right.' Harmful: 'Calm down.' 'As per our policy...' 'There's nothing I can do.' 'You should have...'. The harmful ones all blame or dismiss; the helpful ones acknowledge and act.

## Protect yourself too
Empathy is not endless tolerance. If a customer is abusive, you can stay calm, set a boundary ('I want to help and I'll keep helping, but I'd ask that we keep this respectful'), and escalate to the founder if needed. And use the Week 1 rule: if a message makes you want to fire back, wait. Reply calm, never hot.

cards.prompt: 'I understand your frustration, let me make this right' works better than 'as per our policy...'.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Acknowledge-and-act calms; policy-quoting and blame escalate. Lead with the feeling, then the concrete fix.
cards.whenWrong: Acknowledge-and-act wins. 'Per our policy' reads as a brush-off to an upset person. Validate first, then fix.

cards.prompt: Showing empathy means tolerating any amount of abuse from a customer.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Empathy is not endless tolerance. Stay calm, set a respectful boundary, and escalate genuine abuse to the founder.
cards.whenWrong: No. You can be empathetic and still set a boundary against abuse. Calm respect goes both ways; escalate if it turns abusive.

items.title: De-escalate two hard tickets
items.body:
Write replies that de-escalate:
1. 'This is the WORST shop ever. My order is 3 weeks late, no updates, and now I've missed my mother's birthday. I want a full refund and I'm warning everyone away from you.' (Assume the parcel is delayed but arrives in 2 days.)
2. 'I've emailed twice and no one has replied. Are you even a real business?' (Assume the earlier emails were genuinely missed.)

Use the de-escalation sequence and offer something concrete. Deliverable: the two replies.

days.title: Speed, tone, and prioritising the queue
days.summary: Be fast and consistent, and work the queue by what matters most.

items.title: Running the queue well
items.body:
## Speed matters, within reason
A fast first response calms people, even if the full fix takes longer. A customer who hears back in an hour ('I'm on it, will have an answer by end of day') is calm; one who hears nothing for two days is angry by the time you reach them. Set a response-time standard you can keep (e.g. 'all tickets get a first reply within one business day') and tell customers what to expect.

## Prioritise the queue
Not all tickets are equal. Work by urgency and impact, not just order received:
- **Urgent and high-impact first:** an angry customer, a payment failure, anything time-sensitive (a delivery for an event).
- **Quick wins next:** simple questions you can clear in seconds keep the queue from piling up.
- **Slower, complex ones:** give these proper time, but send a holding reply first so the customer is not left waiting in silence.

## A consistent tone
Every reply should sound like the same warm, competent Kola, whether it is the first ticket of the day or the fiftieth, whether you are fresh or tired. That is what your macros and a short tone guide protect. Consistency is what makes support feel like a real, dependable business rather than one person's mood.

## Do not over-promise
It is tempting to promise a quick fix to make someone happy now. Resist. Promise only what you can deliver, then deliver it. An over-promise that fails ('it'll be there tomorrow' when it won't) does far more damage than an honest 'it'll be 3 days'. Reliability beats optimism every time.

cards.prompt: A fast first response calms a customer even when the full resolution takes longer.
cards.whenRight: Yes. A quick 'I'm on it, answer by end of day' reassures; silence breeds anger. Acknowledge fast, even if the fix takes time.
cards.whenWrong: It does. The first reply's speed is what calms people. A holding response now beats a perfect answer two days of silence later.

cards.prompt: It is better to over-promise a quick fix to make the customer happy now, even if you might not deliver.
cards.whenRight: Correct. A failed over-promise does more damage than an honest longer estimate. Promise only what you can deliver, then deliver it.
cards.whenWrong: No. Over-promising and missing destroys trust. Be honest about timing; reliability beats a hopeful promise you cannot keep.

items.title: Prioritise and set standards
items.body:
1. Given this queue, number them in the order you would work them and say why: a simple shipping question; a furious customer whose event is tomorrow; a payment failure; a restock request; a 'thank you, love my order' message.
2. Write a one-line response-time standard you would commit to and communicate to customers.
3. Write a short tone guide (3 to 5 adjectives with a do/don't example) for Kola support.

Deliverable: the prioritised queue with reasons, the standard, and the tone guide.

days.title: From support to retention
days.summary: Turn good support into loyal customers and fewer tickets over time.

items.title: Support that grows the business
items.body:
## Support is a growth lever, not just a cost
The best operators see support as a way to grow the business, not just to put out fires. Two big moves: turn resolved problems into loyalty, and reduce the tickets that keep happening.

## Turning a save into loyalty
After you fix a problem, a small extra step creates a fan: a follow-up to confirm all is well, a sincere thank-you for their patience, sometimes a small gesture (a discount code, free shipping next time). The customer who had a problem you solved generously will tell people about you. This is far cheaper than winning a new customer and far more powerful than an ad.

## Reduce tickets at the source
Every recurring question is a signal. If 40% of tickets are 'where is my order?', the fix is not faster replies, it is putting clear tracking in the confirmation email and an FAQ on the site, so customers never need to ask. Track which questions repeat, and propose upstream fixes:
- A clear FAQ or help page for the top questions
- Better product photos/descriptions (cuts 'not as pictured' complaints)
- Clear shipping info up front (cuts 'where is it / how much' questions)
- Proactive shipping updates (cuts 'where is my order')

Proposing these makes you more than a ticket-answerer; you become someone improving the business.

## Report the patterns
Part of running support is telling the founder what you are seeing: 'This week, 30% of tickets were about shipping times, here are two things that would cut that in half.' That insight, which only the person in the inbox has, is genuinely valuable and marks you as an operator, not just a responder.

cards.prompt: If the same question keeps coming up, the best fix is just to answer it faster each time.
cards.whenRight: Correct. A recurring question is a signal to fix the cause (add tracking, an FAQ, clearer info) so customers stop needing to ask at all.
cards.whenWrong: Faster answers treat the symptom. The real win is removing the cause upstream so the ticket stops happening. Fix the source, not just the speed.

cards.prompt: Telling the founder which issues are driving the most tickets is valuable insight only the support person has.
cards.whenRight: Yes. You are in the inbox; you see the patterns no one else does. Reporting them (with fixes) marks you as an operator, not just a responder.
cards.whenWrong: It is valuable. The person handling tickets sees patterns the founder cannot. Surfacing them with proposed fixes is high-value operator work.

items.title: Reduce tickets and build loyalty
items.body:
1. From the ticket types this week, identify the two most common and propose a concrete upstream fix for each (e.g. an FAQ entry, a confirmation-email change).
2. Write a follow-up message that turns a resolved complaint into loyalty (with a small gesture).
3. Draft a short FAQ (5 questions and answers) for Kola that would deflect common tickets.

Deliverable: the two fixes, the loyalty follow-up, and the 5-question FAQ.

days.title: Ship: the support simulation
days.summary: Run a full ticket queue and report. Portfolio artefact #7.

items.title: A support operation, packaged
items.body:
## The week's deliverable
Today you run a realistic support week for Kola and package it: a 15-ticket queue worked end to end, your 10+ macro library, customers logged in your CRM, and a short report covering what you handled, how you de-escalated the hard ones, and what would reduce future tickets. This is portfolio artefact number seven.

## Why this sells
Customer support is one of the most available remote roles for someone starting out, because every online business needs it and it can be done from anywhere. Showing that you can run a support operation, fast, warm, consistent, with de-escalation and a retention mindset, makes you immediately hireable. The report, in particular, shows you do not just answer tickets; you think about the customer experience as a whole.

## The standard
Three tests: your replies are warm, specific, and resolve the issue (no robotic non-answers); your hardest ticket is genuinely de-escalated, not just appeased; and your report turns ticket patterns into concrete recommendations. Hit those and a founder would trust you with their customers, which is a real thing to be trusted with.

cards.prompt: Customer support is a strong entry point into remote work because nearly every online business needs it.
cards.whenRight: Yes. It is in constant demand, can be done from anywhere, and a strong support portfolio makes you immediately hireable.
cards.whenWrong: It is a strong entry point. Every online business needs support, it is location-independent, and it is a skill you can demonstrate clearly.

cards.prompt: A great support deliverable just shows fast replies, not any thinking about the wider customer experience.
cards.whenRight: Correct. The report that turns ticket patterns into fixes is what marks you as an operator, not just a responder. Thinking about the whole experience is the value.
cards.whenWrong: Speed alone is not the bar. Showing you analyse patterns and improve the customer experience is what makes the support package genuinely impressive.

items.title: Final build: the support simulation
items.body:
This is the Week 7 portfolio deliverable. Produce:
1. **A worked 15-ticket queue** (mix of orders, questions, complaints, one furious customer), each with your reply, the policy you applied, and its final status.
2. **Your 10+ macro library** and the CRM with the customers logged.
3. **A short support report**: volume by type, how you handled the hardest one, and two recommendations to reduce future tickets.

Export the report and macro library as a PDF. This is portfolio artefact #7.

topics: The support mindset: feeling first, fix second
Setting up a simple help desk and status system
The support reply formula
Building a macro/response library
CRM basics and customer records
Conflict resolution and de-escalation
Speed, tone, and prioritising the queue
From support to retention and reducing tickets
tasks: Set up a support inbox, status system, and simple CRM
Reply to tickets using the support formula
Build a 10+ macro response library
Log customers and use their history
De-escalate angry customers in writing
Prioritise a queue and set a response-time standard
Run a 15-ticket simulation and report patterns
weeks.project: Run a Kola support simulation: a 15-ticket queue worked end to end (including a furious customer), a 10+ macro response library, customers logged in a simple CRM, and a short report on what you handled and what would reduce future tickets. Portfolio artefact #7.
exercises: Reply to five varied tickets using the support formula
Build a 10-macro library with two personalised examples
Build a CRM and write a history-aware reply to a repeat customer
De-escalate two furious customers using the sequence
Prioritise a queue and propose two ticket-reducing fixes
questions: What turns a one-time buyer into a loyal customer through support?
When do you use a macro versus a personal reply?
How do you de-escalate without giving away the business?
outputs: A support report with patterns and recommendations
mastery_questions: Resolve a refund request following a clear, fair policy
Write a support reply using acknowledge, answer/act, next step, warm close
De-escalate an angry customer with the full sequence and a concrete fix
Prioritise a queue by urgency and impact and justify the order
Log a customer interaction and write a history-aware opening line
Turn a resolved complaint into loyalty with a follow-up and a gesture
Write a macro and personalise it for a real ticket
Set and communicate a realistic response-time standard
Identify a recurring ticket type and propose an upstream fix
Report support volume and patterns with two recommendations
weeks.ai_assist: Use AI to draft macros, suggest de-escalation phrasing, and summarise a long customer history before you reply ('summarise this customer's past three tickets'). Ask it to rewrite a reply to sound warmer or more concise. Keep the human firmly in the loop on refunds, exceptions, and anything emotional, an upset customer can instantly tell they are talking to a robot, and that makes it worse. Use AI for speed on the routine; bring your own warmth and judgement to the hard ones.
weeks.pre_flight: Before working the queue, decide your policies and authority: what is the refund rule, what can you offer to make things right (discount, free shipping, replacement), and what must go to the founder? Knowing your limits in advance makes you fast, confident, and consistent instead of stalling on every ticket.
common_mistakes: Leading with policy or blame instead of acknowledging the feeling
Slow first responses that let a small issue grow into anger
Sending a macro verbatim so it reads robotic
Over-promising a fix you cannot deliver
Answering recurring tickets faster instead of fixing their cause
weeks.debug_help: If customers keep escalating, look at your first reply: does it acknowledge the feeling and give a concrete next action with a timeline? Most escalation comes from a first response that felt robotic, slow, or defensive. Lead with a genuine acknowledgement, take ownership, and act specifically. If the same tickets keep coming, stop treating the symptom, fix the cause upstream (FAQ, clearer info, proactive updates) and the volume drops.
stretch: Build a full help-centre / FAQ page to deflect the top tickets
Create a support tone guide so every reply sounds like the same brand
Set up basic automation: an auto-acknowledgement and ticket routing

weeks.title: Social media management
weeks.context:
Many founders need someone to run their social presence, and it is a service you can sell entirely on its own. A small business with a consistent, on-brand feed and someone replying to comments looks alive and trustworthy; one that posts twice a year looks abandoned. This week you learn content operations: planning a content calendar, designing branded graphics in Canva, writing captions that get read, scheduling, community management, and reporting on what worked.

You will manage Kola's social media for a month on paper: a 30-day content calendar, eight branded posts, captions, a scheduling workflow, a brand-voice guide, and an analytics report template. By Friday you can take a business with a dead feed and give it a month of professional content ready to go.

The job is not 'posting'. It is running a small content engine: a plan, a consistent voice, and a habit of looking at what worked and doing more of it.

concept_check.q: Kola posts randomly whenever someone remembers, sometimes three times a week, sometimes nothing for a month. What is the single biggest fix?
choices: Post more often, every single day
A content calendar: plan posts ahead so the feed is consistent and on-purpose
Buy followers
Only post when there is a sale
concept_check.explain: Consistency, driven by a calendar planned in advance, beats sporadic bursts. A plan turns random posting into a reliable presence the audience can count on.

concept_check.q: What decides whether someone stops scrolling on a post?
choices: The number of hashtags
The hook, the first line or first second, which must grab attention immediately
How long the caption is
The time of day only
concept_check.explain: The hook is everything. People decide in a fraction of a second whether to stop. A weak first line means the rest of the post is never seen.

concept_check.q: At the end of the month, which metric is most useful for a small product business?
choices: Total likes across all posts
What actually moved the business: reach, saves/shares, profile visits, link clicks, and sales from social
Number of posts published
Follower count alone
concept_check.explain: Likes are a vanity metric. Useful reporting connects social activity to business outcomes (reach, engagement that signals intent, clicks, sales) and names what to do more of.

days.title: Content operations, and set up your design tool
days.summary: Understand what running social really means, then set up Canva and a brand kit.

items.title: Running a content engine
items.body:
## More than posting
Social media management is not 'making posts'. It is running a small engine with several parts: a strategy (what are we trying to achieve and for whom), a plan (a calendar), production (graphics and captions), distribution (scheduling), community (replying and engaging), and measurement (what worked). A business pays you to run that whole loop so their presence is consistent and purposeful instead of random.

## Start with the goal
Every account exists for a reason: sales, awareness, community, or a mix. Kola's social goal might be 'drive store sales and build a community of people who love handmade West African goods'. The goal shapes everything, what you post, how you measure. Posting with no goal produces busy work that does not move the business.

## Consistency beats intensity
A feed that posts three good times a week, every week, beats one that posts daily for a fortnight then goes silent. Consistency is what an audience (and the algorithm) rewards. Your calendar exists to make consistency easy: plan and create in batches, schedule ahead, and the feed runs even on busy weeks.

## This week's destination
You will produce a month of professional content for Kola: a 30-day calendar, eight branded graphics, captions, a scheduling workflow, a brand-voice guide, and a reporting template. That package is portfolio artefact number eight, and 'I can run your social media' is a service founders pay for monthly, often as a recurring retainer.

items.title: Canva for Social Media: Tutorial for Beginners
items.creator: Maggie Stara
items.why: Maggie Stara is a well-known Canva educator. This concise tutorial shows the exact moves (templates, brand colours, resizing) you will use to make Kola's posts. Watch it, then design your first graphics in the exercise.

items.title: Set up Canva and a brand kit, step by step
items.body:
## Canva is the operator's design tool
You do not need to be a designer. Canva (canva.com, free) gives you templates, drag-and-drop editing, and a library of images and fonts. With it, a non-designer produces clean, on-brand graphics fast.

**1. Sign up** free at canva.com.

**2. Learn the basics:** search a template (e.g. 'Instagram post'), pick one, and edit, click any element to change text, colour, or image; drag to move; use the resize option to turn one design into other sizes (a post into a story). Spend ten minutes just clicking around; it is intuitive.

**3. Define the brand basics.** A brand looks consistent when it reuses the same few elements. For Kola, decide: two or three brand colours (note their hex codes), one or two fonts, and the logo. On Canva's free plan you keep these in a simple reference doc (the paid Brand Kit feature stores them, but a doc works fine). Every graphic uses these, so the feed looks like one brand, not a random collage.

**4. Make one test graphic** using a template, swapped to Kola's colours, with a real product photo and a short headline. That is the workflow you will repeat all week.

## Why consistency in design matters
When every post shares the same colours, fonts, and feel, the feed becomes instantly recognisable, a customer scrolling sees a Kola post and knows it is Kola before reading a word. That visual consistency is a huge part of looking like a real, established brand rather than a hobby.

cards.prompt: Posting daily for two weeks then going silent for a month is better than posting three times a week consistently.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Consistency beats intensity. A steady three-times-a-week rhythm builds audience and algorithm trust; bursts then silence loses both.
cards.whenWrong: The other way. Steady consistency wins. Bursts followed by silence make an account look abandoned and lose momentum with the audience and the algorithm.

cards.prompt: Reusing the same few brand colours and fonts across posts makes a feed look more professional.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Visual consistency makes the brand instantly recognisable, a Kola post looks like Kola before you read it, which signals an established business.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Consistent colours and fonts make the feed cohesive and recognisable. A random mix of styles looks like a hobby, not a brand.

items.title: Your turn, set up the design system
items.body:
- [ ] Sign up for Canva (free)
- [ ] Define Kola's brand basics in a doc: 2 to 3 colours (with hex codes), 1 to 2 fonts, and where the logo lives
- [ ] Make one test Instagram post from a template, swapped to Kola's colours, with a product photo and a short headline
- [ ] Resize that design into a second format (e.g. a story) to see the resize feature

Deliverable: your brand-basics doc and the test graphic (exported as an image).

days.title: Content strategy and the calendar
days.summary: Plan a month of posts on purpose, not on a whim.

items.title: The content calendar
items.body:
## Plan, then create
Trying to think of a post in the moment, every day, is exhausting and produces weak content. The professional move is to plan a batch ahead (a week or a month) in a content calendar, then create and schedule in focused sessions. The calendar removes the daily 'what do I post?' panic.

## Content pillars
A feed of nothing but 'buy our product' is boring and people tune out. Strong accounts rotate a few content pillars, recurring themes that serve the audience. For Kola, pillars might be:
- **Product:** showcase items, new arrivals, details.
- **Behind the scenes:** the makers, the craft, the story (huge for a handmade brand).
- **Educational/value:** how to style a piece, the meaning behind a pattern, care tips.
- **Social proof:** customer photos, reviews, testimonials.
- **Community/culture:** celebrations, heritage, the people behind the brand.

Rotating pillars keeps the feed varied and gives the audience reasons to follow beyond just buying.

## Build the calendar
A content calendar is a simple table (Sheet or Notion): one row per post, with the date, the pillar, the format (image, carousel, reel, story), the topic, the caption, the graphic status, and where it links. Plan a realistic cadence (e.g. four posts a week) and assign each a pillar so the mix stays balanced. Now you can see the month at a glance and the feed has intention.

## Plan around the calendar that matters
Anchor content to real events: a holiday sale (December, Week 6), a restock, a cultural celebration, a product launch. Planning ahead means the launch posts are ready before the launch, not scrambled the night before.

cards.prompt: A strong feed rotates a few content pillars rather than only posting 'buy our product'.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Pillars (product, behind-the-scenes, value, social proof, community) keep the feed varied and give people reasons to follow beyond buying.
cards.whenWrong: Pillars win. An all-sales feed gets tuned out. Rotating themes serves the audience and keeps them engaged between purchases.

cards.prompt: Planning content in a calendar ahead of time produces better posts than improvising daily.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Batch planning removes the daily panic and lets you create thoughtfully and consistently, which shows in the quality.
cards.whenWrong: It does. A calendar lets you plan and batch-create, which is calmer and better than scrambling for an idea every single day.

items.title: Build a 2-week content calendar
items.body:
1. Define Kola's social goal in one sentence and list 4 to 5 content pillars.
2. Build a content-calendar table (date, pillar, format, topic, caption, graphic status, link).
3. Fill two weeks (e.g. 8 posts) with a balanced mix of pillars and at least one tied to an event (a restock or sale).

Deliverable: the two-week content calendar.

days.title: Designing graphics in Canva
days.summary: Produce clean, on-brand visuals that stop the scroll.

items.title: Design that works on a feed
items.body:
## You are not making art, you are stopping a scroll
A social graphic has one job: make someone pause. It competes in a fast-moving feed, so clarity and contrast beat clever and busy. A few principles take a non-designer a long way:

- **One message per graphic.** Do not cram. One clear idea, one focal point. If you have three things to say, that is three posts or a carousel.
- **Readable text.** Big enough to read on a phone, high contrast against the background, short. If a headline does not fit in a glance, cut it.
- **Strong focal image.** A great product photo does most of the work. Good light, clean background. Poor photos sink good design.
- **Breathing room.** White space makes a design feel premium. Cramped designs feel cheap.
- **On-brand always.** Your colours and fonts on every graphic (Day 0). Consistency over novelty.

## Work from templates
Do not start from a blank canvas. Pick a Canva template close to what you want and adapt it, swap colours to your brand, replace the image, rewrite the text. Templates carry good design choices (balance, hierarchy) you do not have to invent. This is how non-designers produce professional-looking work fast.

## Formats
Know the main shapes: a square/portrait feed post, a vertical story, a carousel (multiple swipeable images, great for teaching or showing a range), and a reel cover. Canva resizes between them. A carousel that teaches something (e.g. 'how to style a Kola basket, 5 ways') often gets saved and shared, which the algorithm loves.

## Batch it
Make a week or month of graphics in one focused session, reusing your template and brand elements. Batching is far faster than making one at a time and keeps the look consistent.

cards.prompt: Cramming several messages and lots of text onto one graphic makes it more effective.
cards.whenRight: Correct. One message per graphic. A busy, text-heavy design loses people; clarity and a single focal point stop the scroll.
cards.whenWrong: It backfires. Crammed graphics get skipped. One clear idea, readable text, and breathing room is what works in a fast feed.

cards.prompt: Starting from a Canva template is a smart way for a non-designer to produce professional graphics.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Templates carry good design choices you adapt (brand colours, your photo, your text), so you get professional results fast without designing from scratch.
cards.whenWrong: It is smart. Templates bake in balance and hierarchy. Adapting one to your brand beats a blank canvas every time for a non-designer.

items.title: Design three on-brand graphics
items.body:
Using Canva and Kola's brand basics, design three graphics for your calendar:
1. A product feature post.
2. A behind-the-scenes or story-of-the-maker post.
3. A carousel that teaches something (e.g. '5 ways to style this piece') with at least 3 slides.

Apply the principles: one message each, readable text, on-brand colours. Deliverable: the three exported graphics.

days.title: Captions and hooks
days.summary: Write the words that make people stop, read, and act.

items.title: The hook is everything
items.body:
## The first line decides the rest
People scroll fast. The first line of a caption (and the first second of a video) decides whether they stop. A weak opener means the best caption in the world goes unread. So the hook gets your sharpest effort.

Weak openers: 'We're excited to announce...', 'Check out our new...'. Strong hooks create curiosity, name a benefit, ask a real question, or start a story:
- 'This basket took three weeks and four generations of skill to make.'
- 'The mistake everyone makes when styling woven decor (and the easy fix).'
- 'We almost didn't restock this one. Here's why we did.'

## Caption structure
After the hook: deliver on it (the story, the value, the detail), then a clear **call to action (CTA)**, the one thing you want the reader to do. 'Shop the link in bio.' 'Comment your favourite.' 'Save this for later.' 'Tag someone who'd love this.' A caption with no CTA is a missed chance; every post should ask for one specific action.

## Voice and length
Write in the brand's voice (warm and a little playful for Kola), like a person, not a press release. Length depends on the goal: short and punchy for a quick product post, longer and story-driven for behind-the-scenes or value content (longer captions that genuinely engage can boost reach). Either way, make the first line earn the read.

## Hashtags and details, briefly
Hashtags help discovery; use a handful of relevant ones (a mix of broad and niche), not thirty. They are a minor lever, the content and hook matter far more. Put them at the end or in a first comment to keep the caption clean.

## Repurpose one idea many ways
A single idea ('the story of our weavers') becomes a feed post, a carousel, a story, and a reel, each with a tailored hook. Repurposing is how you fill a calendar without inventing endless new ideas.

cards.prompt: 'We're excited to announce our new product!' is a strong opening hook.
cards.whenRight: Correct. That is a weak, generic opener. Strong hooks spark curiosity, name a benefit, ask a real question, or start a story.
cards.whenWrong: It is weak. 'Excited to announce' is forgettable. Lead with curiosity, a benefit, or a story so people actually stop scrolling.

cards.prompt: Every post should include a clear call to action telling the reader one thing to do.
cards.whenRight: Yes. A CTA (shop, comment, save, tag) turns passive scrolling into action. A post with no CTA wastes the attention it earned.
cards.whenWrong: It should. The CTA is how a post does work, shop, comment, save, share. Without it you got attention and asked for nothing.

items.title: Write five captions with hooks
items.body:
For five posts in your calendar, write full captions, each with:
1. A scroll-stopping first line (hook).
2. The body that delivers on the hook, in Kola's voice.
3. One clear call to action.

Then take ONE idea and write three different hooks for it (for a post, a carousel, and a reel). Deliverable: the five captions plus the three hooks for one idea.

days.title: Scheduling and workflow
days.summary: Set posts to publish on their own so the feed runs without you live.

items.title: Schedule ahead, free your time
items.body:
## Why schedule
Posting manually at the 'right' time every day chains you to your phone and breaks the moment you are busy or offline. Scheduling tools let you load a week or month of posts in one session and have them publish automatically. This is what makes managing social for several clients possible, and what keeps a feed consistent through holidays and busy weeks.

## The tools
- **Meta Business Suite** (free) schedules posts and stories to Facebook and Instagram, and is the native, reliable option for those platforms. It also holds the analytics and the unified inbox for comments and DMs.
- **Buffer** (free tier) schedules across multiple platforms from one place, with a simple calendar view. Good when a client is on several networks.
- Others (Later, Hootsuite) do similar things. Learn one; the concepts transfer.

## The workflow
1. Plan in your content calendar (Day 1).
2. Batch-create graphics (Day 2) and captions (Day 3).
3. Load everything into the scheduler with dates and times.
4. Review the scheduled queue (right post, right caption, right time, link working).
5. Let it publish, and spend your live time on community, not posting.

## Timing, lightly
Post when your audience is active; the platform's analytics will tell you when that is. But do not obsess, consistency and content quality matter far more than hitting a 'perfect' minute. Pick reasonable times, stay consistent, and let the data refine it over a few weeks.

## Always review before it goes out
Scheduled does not mean unchecked. A typo, a wrong link, or a post that lands badly on a sensitive day can go out automatically if you do not review the queue. Glance over what is scheduled, especially around real-world events, so nothing tone-deaf publishes on its own.

cards.prompt: Scheduling posts in advance lets the feed stay consistent even when you are busy or offline.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Batch-load a week or month and it publishes itself, which is how you keep consistency and manage social for multiple clients.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Scheduling decouples posting from your live availability, so the feed runs through busy weeks and holidays without you.

cards.prompt: Once posts are scheduled you never need to look at the queue again.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Always review the queue: a typo, broken link, or a post landing on a sensitive day can publish automatically. Scheduled is not unchecked.
cards.whenWrong: You do need to review. Auto-publishing means mistakes (or tone-deaf timing) go out on their own unless you glance over the queue, especially around real events.

items.title: Set up a scheduling workflow
items.body:
1. Set up Meta Business Suite or Buffer (free) and connect a test/sample account, or document the steps if you cannot connect a live account.
2. Schedule (or mock-schedule) your week of posts with dates, times, captions, and links.
3. Write your batching workflow as a short checklist (plan, create graphics, write captions, schedule, review).

Deliverable: a screenshot of the scheduled queue (or the documented steps) plus your workflow checklist.

days.title: Community management
days.summary: Reply, engage, and turn followers into a community.

items.title: The conversation is half the job
items.body:
## Posting is half; engaging is the other half
An account that posts but never replies is a billboard, not a community. The accounts people love feel alive: comments get answered, DMs get warm replies, the brand acts like a person. Community management, the engagement side, is what turns followers into customers and customers into advocates.

## What it involves
- **Reply to comments**, warmly and in brand voice. Even a quick 'thank you!' or a real answer to a question makes people feel seen and signals an active brand. Questions in comments are buying signals, answer them fast.
- **Handle DMs**, which are often support or sales in disguise ('is this in stock?', 'do you ship to X?'). Treat them with the same care as support tickets (Week 7).
- **Engage outward.** Like and thoughtfully comment on customers' and partners' posts. A brand that engages with its community gets engagement back.
- **Encourage and reshare user content.** When a customer posts your product, thank them and (with permission) reshare it. This social proof is the most persuasive content you have, and it costs nothing.

## Tone and speed
Match the platform's casual energy while staying on-brand. And speed matters: a comment or DM answered within hours keeps momentum (and can close a sale); one answered three days later is a missed opportunity. Build a habit of checking and clearing the social inbox daily, like email.

## Handle negativity calmly
Public criticism happens. The Week 7 de-escalation skills apply: acknowledge, do not get defensive, and offer to take it to DM to resolve ('So sorry to hear this, can you DM us your order number? We'll make it right.'). Handled well in public, a complaint becomes a demonstration that the brand cares. Never argue publicly.

## Watch for the line
Engagement is genuine relationship-building, not spam. Real, specific replies beat copy-pasted emojis. The goal is a community that feels personally connected to the brand, which is something no ad can buy.

cards.prompt: A brand should argue back publicly when it receives a critical comment.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Never argue publicly. Acknowledge calmly, avoid defensiveness, and offer to resolve it in DMs. Handled well, a complaint shows the brand cares.
cards.whenWrong: No. Public arguments damage the brand. Acknowledge, stay calm, and move it to DM to fix, the Week 7 de-escalation approach.

cards.prompt: A question in the comments or DMs is often a buying signal worth answering fast.
cards.whenRight: Yes. 'Is this in stock?' is a customer ready to buy. A fast, warm reply can close the sale; a slow one loses it.
cards.whenWrong: It usually is. Questions about stock, shipping, or price are interest signals. Answering quickly and warmly often converts; delay loses the moment.

items.title: Practise community management
items.body:
Write replies (in Kola's voice) to:
1. A comment: 'This is gorgeous! Do you ship to the UK?'
2. A DM: 'Is the large basket back in stock?'
3. A customer who posted a photo of their Kola purchase.
4. A public negative comment: 'Ordered weeks ago, still nothing. Disappointed.'

Then write a one-line daily community-management routine (what you check and do each day). Deliverable: the four replies and the routine.

days.title: Analytics and reporting
days.summary: Measure what matters and turn it into next month's plan.

items.title: Reading the numbers, and acting on them
items.body:
## Measure what matters, not vanity
Likes feel good but rarely move a business. Useful social measurement connects activity to outcomes:
- **Reach / impressions:** how many people saw it (awareness).
- **Engagement that signals intent:** saves and shares (people found it valuable enough to keep or pass on) matter more than likes; comments show real interest.
- **Profile visits and link clicks:** people moving toward buying.
- **Follower growth:** slow and steady from good content beats spikes from giveaways.
- **Sales attributed to social:** the ultimate metric, tracked via link clicks, discount codes, or 'how did you hear about us'.

The native analytics (Meta Business Suite, Instagram Insights) give you these for free.

## The real skill: so what
Numbers alone are not a report. The value is interpretation: which posts performed best and why, and what to do more of. 'The behind-the-scenes weaver post got 3x the saves and shares of our product posts, people connect with the story, so next month we'll do more maker content' is a real, actionable finding. That is what a founder wants, not a screenshot of likes.

## The monthly report
Pull it together monthly (BLUF, like every report this course): a headline (growth and what drove it), the key numbers, the top posts and why they worked, and one or two recommendations for next month. Keep it to a page. A consistent monthly report makes you look like a strategist, not just a poster, and it justifies the retainer.

## Let data feed the calendar
The loop closes here: what worked this month shapes next month's content pillars and calendar. Double down on the formats and topics that performed; quietly drop what did not. Over a few months this data-driven adjustment compounds into real growth, which is the difference between busy posting and effective social management.

cards.prompt: Saves and shares are often more meaningful than likes for a small business.
cards.whenRight: Yes. A save means someone wanted to keep it; a share means they passed it on. Both signal real value and reach far more than a like.
cards.whenWrong: They are. Likes are easy and shallow; saves and shares show people found the content valuable enough to keep or spread, which matters more.

cards.prompt: A good monthly report is just a screenshot of the follower count and total likes.
cards.whenRight: Correct. The value is interpretation: which posts worked, why, and what to do next month. Raw vanity numbers with no 'so what' are not a report.
cards.whenWrong: Not enough. A report explains what worked and why and recommends next steps. Screenshots of likes leave the founder with no decision to make.

items.title: Build a monthly report template
items.body:
1. Build a one-page monthly social report template with sections: headline (growth + driver), key metrics (reach, engagement, saves/shares, clicks, followers), top 3 posts and why they worked, and 2 recommendations for next month.
2. Fill it with realistic invented numbers for Kola and write a genuine 'so what' for the top post.

Deliverable: the filled report and the blank reusable template.

days.title: Ship: a month of social media
days.summary: Deliver a complete content package for Kola. Portfolio artefact #8.

items.title: A content engine, packaged
items.body:
## The week's deliverable
Today you package a full month of social media management for Kola: a 30-day content calendar, eight branded graphics, captions, a scheduling workflow, a brand-voice guide, and a monthly report template. This is portfolio artefact number eight, and it is the kind of work clients pay a monthly retainer for.

## Why this is sellable on its own
Social media management is one of the most common standalone services a remote operator sells, because almost every small business needs it, knows they are bad at it, and would happily pay someone to take it off their plate. A complete month of content, planned, designed, captioned, scheduled, and measured, is concrete proof you can run a brand's presence. Show this package and 'can you run our Instagram?' becomes an easy yes.

## The standard
Three tests: the feed looks like one consistent brand (same colours, fonts, voice across every post); the content has variety and purpose (pillars, not all sales); and there is a measurement loop (a report that turns numbers into next month's plan). Hit those and you are not a poster, you are a social media manager.

cards.prompt: Social media management is commonly sold as a standalone monthly retainer service.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Most small businesses need it, know they neglect it, and will pay monthly for someone to run it well. It is a strong standalone offering.
cards.whenWrong: It is. Recurring social management is a classic operator service, businesses pay a monthly retainer because they need consistency they cannot keep themselves.

cards.prompt: A complete content package needs a measurement loop, not just nice posts.
cards.whenRight: Yes. The report that turns results into next month's plan is what separates a social media manager from someone who just posts. Measurement is the strategist's part.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Pretty posts without measurement is guessing. The loop, measure, learn, adjust the calendar, is what makes the management strategic and effective.
