weeks.title: Real client experience, part 2
weeks.context:
Part 2 is the deep end. You will deliver a local business project and run a full founder-assistant simulation: operating as Ama's right hand for a simulated week, juggling inbox, calendar, tasks, research, and support all at once, while a couple of urgent things go wrong. This is the closest thing to the real job, and it is where everything from Weeks 1 to 11 has to work together under realistic pressure.

The new skill this week is integration: prioritising across competing demands, switching contexts without dropping balls, and operating proactively (anticipating needs, not just reacting). You will also learn to capture your work as case studies, because the difference between having done great work and being able to prove it is the story you can tell about it.

Under load, the operators who stay calm are not the ones with the best memory; they are the ones whose system catches the balls so their head stays clear. This week tests exactly that.

concept_check.q: It's a busy simulated day: an angry customer, a report due, a meeting to book, and the founder asking for research, all at once. What do you do first?
choices: Whatever landed most recently
Triage by urgency and impact: handle what is time-critical and high-impact first, send holding replies on the rest, and communicate what will wait
Try to do all four simultaneously
The easiest one, to feel productive
concept_check.explain: Under load you triage by urgency and impact, not by what is loudest or easiest. Handle the critical first, acknowledge the rest with holding replies, and communicate what waits.

concept_check.q: What does operating 'proactively' look like for a founder's assistant?
choices: Doing exactly what you are told, quickly
Anticipating needs and acting before being asked, e.g. preparing the meeting brief before the founder requests it
Asking the founder what to do at every step
Waiting for instructions to avoid mistakes
concept_check.explain: Proactive operation means anticipating what the founder will need and handling it ahead of time. That foresight is what separates a great assistant from a merely competent one.

concept_check.q: Why write case studies of your engagements?
choices: To pad your portfolio with text
Because being able to clearly tell the story of a problem you solved (situation, action, result) is what wins the next client or job
Clients require them by law
They are not actually useful
concept_check.explain: A case study turns work you did into proof you can sell: situation, action, result. The ability to tell that story is often what lands the next opportunity.

days.title: The founder-assistant role, and set up for the simulation
days.summary: Understand what it means to be someone's right hand, then set up your system to run a full week of it.

items.title: Being someone's right hand
items.body:
## The integrated role
So far you practised skills one at a time and ran focused engagements. The founder-assistant role is all of it at once: you are the person a founder relies on to keep everything running, inbox, calendar, tasks, research, support, reporting, whatever the day brings. It is the role this whole course has been building toward, and the most valuable, because you take the widest possible load off the founder.

## What changes when it is everything at once
- **You constantly prioritise.** With many demands, you decide what matters most, right now, all day. Prioritisation becomes your core skill.
- **You context-switch.** From an angry customer to a calendar to a report to research, cleanly, without dropping the thread on any of them. Your system, not your memory, holds it together.
- **You operate proactively.** You do not just react to requests; you anticipate what the founder will need and have it ready.
- **You stay calm under load.** Things go wrong; the founder watches how you handle it. Calm, communicated control is the product.

## This week's two pieces
1. **A local business project:** another real client type (a shop, a restaurant, a service business), often less tech-savvy, very practical needs. You scope and deliver it like Week 11.
2. **The founder-assistant simulation:** a simulated week as Ama's right hand, a realistic mix of daily work plus a couple of curveballs, run with your full system.

## This week's destination
The delivered local-business project, a completed simulation log showing how you handled a real week, and case studies of your best work, consolidating everything into a portfolio that proves you can run a founder's operations. After this, Week 13 turns it all into a job or clients.

items.title: Set up to run a whole week, step by step
items.body:
## Your system is what makes this possible
You cannot hold a founder's entire operation in your head, that is the whole point of the systems you built. Before the simulation, get your system ready so that when the week gets busy, nothing is lost.

**1. One capture inbox.** Every incoming thing (a request, an email, an idea, a problem) lands in one place (your task board's inbox from Week 2). Under load, capture-first is non-negotiable, the moment something arrives, it goes into the system, not your memory.

**2. A daily plan with priorities.** Each morning of the simulation, turn the load into a time-blocked plan (Week 2), with your two or three most important things first. Re-plan as the day throws curveballs.

**3. A status surface for the founder.** A place (a shared board, a daily update) where Ama can see what is handled, in progress, and waiting, so she stays calm without asking.

**4. Your toolkits ready.** Your communication templates, support macros, prompt library, SOPs, all the assets you built are now your speed. Have them at hand so you respond fast.

## Rehearse the rhythm
Plan to run the simulation as a real working rhythm: a morning plan, focused work blocks, regular capture and triage, an end-of-day update. Set this up now so the simulation tests your operating system under pressure, which is exactly what a real founder engagement will do.

cards.prompt: Under a heavy workload, capturing every incoming task into one system the moment it arrives is non-negotiable.
cards.whenRight: Yes. When it is busy, memory fails fastest. Capture-first into one inbox is what keeps balls from dropping while you focus on the task at hand.
cards.whenWrong: It is non-negotiable. The busier it gets, the more you must trust the system over your head. Capture everything immediately, decide later.

cards.prompt: A founder-assistant's core skill, when handling everything at once, is constant prioritisation.
cards.whenRight: Yes. With many competing demands, deciding what matters most right now, all day, is the central skill. The system holds the rest.
cards.whenWrong: It is. Doing everything is impossible; deciding what matters most at each moment is the job. Prioritisation is the founder-assistant's core muscle.

items.title: Your turn, set up the operating system
items.body:
- [ ] Confirm your capture inbox (one place all incoming work lands)
- [ ] Prepare a daily-plan template with a priorities section
- [ ] Set up a status surface the 'founder' can see (board or daily update format)
- [ ] Gather your toolkits (templates, macros, prompts, SOPs) so they're at hand
- [ ] Choose a local business and a concrete project for it

Deliverable: your ready operating system and the chosen local-business project.

days.title: Prioritising across competing demands
days.summary: Decide what matters most when everything is asking for attention.

items.title: Triage like an operator
items.body:
## The skill that defines the role
When you run everything, the hardest and most valuable thing you do is decide what to work on when ten things compete. Get this right and the important things happen and the founder feels on top of it all; get it wrong and you are busy all day while the thing that mattered slips.

## Triage by urgency and impact
Judge each demand on two axes:
- **Urgency:** how time-sensitive is it? (A customer's event tomorrow; a payment failure; a report due in an hour.)
- **Impact:** how much does it matter to the goal/business? (A big client at risk vs a minor formatting tweak.)

Roughly: do the urgent-and-high-impact first; schedule the important-but-not-urgent (and protect that time, this is where the valuable proactive work lives); knock out or batch the quick low-impact things; and question or drop the low-urgency, low-impact noise. The classic trap is spending the day on urgent-but-trivial things while the important-not-urgent work (that actually moves the business) never gets done.

## Communicate what waits
You cannot do everything at once, and that is fine, as long as you communicate. When you prioritise one thing over another, send a holding reply on what waits: 'On it, will have this to you by 2pm' or 'Got your request, I'm handling an urgent customer issue first, yours by end of day, shout if it's more urgent.' Communicated triage feels handled; silent triage feels ignored. The difference is one sentence.

## Re-prioritise as the day changes
A plan made at 9am rarely survives to noon. New urgent things land; priorities shift. Re-triage calmly when they do, do not rigidly stick to a stale plan, and do not panic. The skill is fluid, judgement-based reprioritising, all day, while keeping the founder informed of what that means for their expectations.

cards.prompt: The classic trap is spending all day on urgent-but-trivial tasks while important-not-urgent work never gets done.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Urgency screams; importance whispers. Protecting time for important-not-urgent work (the proactive, business-moving stuff) is what separates great operators.
cards.whenWrong: It is the classic trap. The loud urgent-trivial things eat the day while the important work that actually matters keeps getting deferred. Protect it.

cards.prompt: When you prioritise one task over another, sending a quick holding reply on what waits makes the difference between feeling handled and feeling ignored.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Communicated triage feels handled; silent triage feels ignored. One sentence ('on it, yours by 2pm') is the whole difference.
cards.whenWrong: It does. You can't do everything at once, but a holding reply tells people they're not forgotten. Silence is what makes triage feel like neglect.

items.title: Triage a chaotic morning
items.body:
It's 9am for Ama and these all land at once: a furious customer whose order is for an event tomorrow; the monthly report due to a partner by noon; three new customer questions; Ama asking for quick research on a new courier; a supplier needing a deposit confirmed; and a teammate blocked waiting on you.
1. Order them by what you'd do, with a one-line reason each (urgency x impact).
2. Write the holding replies you'd send for the things that must wait.

Deliverable: the prioritised order with reasons and the holding replies.

days.title: Context-switching without dropping balls
days.summary: Move between very different tasks while keeping every thread.

items.title: Switching cleanly
items.body:
## The cost of switching
A founder-assistant switches contexts constantly: a tense customer reply, then a calendar, then a spreadsheet, then research, then a quick decision. Each switch has a cost, a moment of 'where was I?', and the risk that something half-done gets forgotten. Managing that cost is a real skill.

## How to switch without dropping anything
- **Close the loop or capture the open thread before you switch.** If you must leave a task half-done, write down exactly where you stopped and the next step, in the task. Then when you return, you resume instantly instead of reconstructing. Never leave an open thread only in your head when you switch.
- **Batch similar work when you can.** Instead of switching for every single email, batch all email into a block, all calls into another. Fewer switches, less cost. Some interruptions are unavoidable; reduce the avoidable ones.
- **Protect focus for the deep task.** When something needs real concentration (a report, a plan), defend a block for it and let the routine queue, you will do the routine faster afterward anyway.
- **Trust the system, not your head.** With everything captured (Day 0), switching is safe: nothing is lost because nothing lives only in your memory. This is why the system matters most exactly when it is busy.

## The end-of-task habit
When you finish (or pause) any task, take three seconds: update its status, note any follow-up, and glance at what's next. This tiny ritual keeps the whole operation current and means you always know your real state, no nasty surprises, no 'I completely forgot about that'.

## Calm is a choice the system enables
Frantic switching, where you feel scattered and afraid of forgetting, comes from relying on memory. Calm switching comes from trusting a system that holds everything. The founder feels which one you are: a scattered assistant makes them nervous; a calm one, who clearly has it all captured, makes them relax. Your system is what produces that calm.

cards.prompt: Before switching away from a half-done task, you should note where you stopped and the next step.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Capturing the open thread means you resume instantly and never forget it. Leaving it only in your head is how half-done work gets dropped.
cards.whenWrong: You should. A quick 'stopped here, next step is X' note lets you return cleanly and guarantees the task is not forgotten in the shuffle.

cards.prompt: Calm context-switching comes from a good memory, not from a system.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Calm comes from trusting a system that holds everything; relying on memory is what makes switching frantic and risky. The system produces the calm.
cards.whenWrong: It comes from the system, not memory. When everything is captured, switching is safe and calm. Memory-reliance is exactly what makes it frantic.

items.title: Switch cleanly through a sequence
items.body:
Simulate a sequence: you're writing the monthly report when (1) an urgent customer email arrives, then (2) Ama pings for a quick decision, then (3) you return to the report.
1. Write what you capture/note at each switch so nothing is dropped.
2. Describe how you'd batch or protect focus to minimise the switching cost.

Deliverable: the switch-notes for each transition and your batching/focus approach.

days.title: Operating proactively
days.summary: Anticipate needs and act before being asked.

items.title: Anticipation is the senior skill
items.body:
## Reactive vs proactive
A competent assistant does what they are asked, well. A great one anticipates what will be needed and handles it before being asked. That foresight is the single biggest thing that elevates an assistant from helpful to indispensable, and it is what justifies higher trust and higher pay.

## What proactive looks like
- **Prepare ahead.** The founder has a meeting at 2pm? The brief, the relevant docs, and any prep are ready on their desk by 1pm, without them asking. They mention a supplier visit next month? You've started the itinerary.
- **Spot and surface issues early.** You notice a deadline that will collide, a customer going quiet, a low-stock item that will sell out, and you flag it (with a suggestion) before it becomes a fire.
- **Remove future friction.** You see a question customers keep asking and propose an FAQ; you notice a recurring manual task and suggest a fix (Weeks 7 and 9). You're improving the operation, not just running it.
- **Think one step ahead.** For every task, ask 'what will the founder need next because of this?' and tee it up. Booked the flight? Prepare the itinerary. Finished the report? Draft the message that sends it on.

## How to become proactive
Proactivity grows from understanding the business and the founder. The more you learn how Ama works, what she cares about, what's coming up, the better you anticipate. Keep a running awareness (your notes, the calendar, the patterns you see) and regularly ask yourself 'what's coming that I could get ahead of?'. Early on you'll anticipate a little; with familiarity, a lot.

## Proactive, not overstepping
There's a line: anticipate and prepare, but do not make significant or irreversible decisions that are the founder's to make. The skill is teeing things up and surfacing options ('I noticed X and drafted a response, want me to send it?'), so the founder gets the benefit of your foresight while keeping the decisions that are theirs. That balance, initiative with judgement, is exactly what the most trusted operators master.

cards.prompt: Anticipating what a founder will need and preparing it before they ask is what elevates an assistant from helpful to indispensable.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Foresight is the senior skill. Having the meeting brief ready before it's requested is what earns the highest trust and pay.
cards.whenWrong: It is the elevating skill. Reacting well is good; anticipating and preparing ahead is what makes a founder feel they can't run things without you.

cards.prompt: Being proactive means making the founder's significant decisions for them to save their time.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Anticipate and tee things up, but keep the founder's decisions theirs. Surface options ('I drafted this, want me to send it?'); don't overstep on irreversible calls.
cards.whenWrong: That oversteps. Proactivity is preparing and surfacing options, not making the founder's big or irreversible decisions. Initiative with judgement is the balance.

items.title: Practise anticipation
items.body:
For each situation, write the proactive move (what you'd prepare or surface before being asked):
1. Ama has an investor call Thursday.
2. A best-selling product is down to 12 units.
3. The same customer question has come up five times this week.
4. Ama mentioned wanting to 'do something for the holidays' next month.

For each, also note where you'd stop and surface a decision rather than act alone. Deliverable: the four proactive moves with their decision-points.

days.title: Delivering for a local business
days.summary: Serve a practical, often less tech-savvy client well.

items.title: Operating for a local business
items.body:
## A different client again
A local business, a shop, a restaurant, a salon, a tradesperson, is another flavour of client. Often the owner is very busy with the hands-on work, less comfortable with tech, and has practical, immediate needs rather than abstract strategy. The opportunity is huge: many local businesses are drowning in admin and have never considered remote help.

## How to deliver well here
- **Be practical and concrete.** They want problems solved, not jargon. 'I'll set up online booking so you stop losing appointments to missed calls' beats 'I'll optimise your customer-acquisition funnel'. Speak their language.
- **Keep it simple and low-maintenance.** A less tech-savvy owner needs solutions they can actually use and sustain. Favour the simplest tool that works, and document it plainly (Week 9 SOPs, written for someone non-technical).
- **Show quick, tangible wins.** Sort their inbox, set up a booking system, organise their supplier orders, something they feel immediately. Local owners are sceptical of 'online help'; a fast concrete result wins them over.
- **Respect how they work.** They built the business their way; come in helping, not lecturing. Understand their reality (busy, hands-on, practical) and fit your help to it.

## A concrete local-business deliverable
Pick a real, useful project. Examples: set up and organise their customer enquiries (a simple inbox + response system + a booking or order process); build a basic system to track orders/appointments/stock; create simple social media or a Google Business Profile presence; or document their key processes so a new staff member can be trained. Deliver one of these fully and simply, with plain documentation they can keep using.

## Why this client type matters for you
Local businesses are an accessible, often-overlooked market, especially close to home. Serving one well proves you can adapt to a non-technical, practical client and deliver real, felt value, and it may be exactly where your first paying clients come from. Adapting across a startup, an NGO, and a local business shows the full range that makes you hireable anywhere.

cards.prompt: With a less tech-savvy local business owner, you should favour the simplest tool that works and document it plainly.
cards.whenRight: Yes. They need solutions they can actually use and sustain. Simple tools plus plain, non-technical documentation is what serves them, not the fanciest option.
cards.whenWrong: Simple wins here. A non-technical owner needs maintainable solutions and clear plain-language docs, the fanciest tool they can't sustain is useless.

cards.prompt: Speaking in marketing jargon ('optimise your acquisition funnel') impresses a local business owner.
cards.whenRight: Correct. It alienates them. Be concrete: 'I'll set up online booking so you stop losing appointments.' Plain, practical language earns their trust.
cards.whenWrong: It does the opposite. Jargon creates distance. Local owners respond to concrete, practical descriptions of the problem you'll solve.

items.title: Deliver the local-business project
items.body:
1. Choose a local business type and a concrete, practical project (e.g. enquiry/booking system, order tracking, simple social presence, process docs for staff).
2. Deliver it fully and simply, using sustainable tools.
3. Write plain, non-technical documentation the owner could follow.
4. Note one quick tangible win you delivered early.

Deliverable: the delivered project, the plain documentation, and the early-win note.

days.title: Performing under pressure
days.summary: Stay calm and effective when things go wrong mid-week.

items.title: When the curveballs come
items.body:
## Real weeks have fires
No real week goes to plan. Mid-simulation, things will go wrong: a furious customer escalates, the website goes down, a supplier cancels, two deadlines collide, the founder dumps an urgent new priority on you at 4pm. How you handle pressure is what a founder is really paying to find out, because the calm days do not need you nearly as much as the chaotic ones.

## The under-pressure playbook
1. **Pause and assess, do not react blindly.** Ten seconds to see the whole picture beats instantly grabbing the loudest thing. What's actually most urgent and important?
2. **Triage and sequence** (Day 1). Handle the critical first; hold the rest with quick replies.
3. **Communicate proactively.** Tell the founder what's happening, what you're doing, and what (if anything) you need from them: 'Website's down, I've contacted the host and posted a holding note on social, will update you in 20 min.' A founder who knows you're on it relaxes; one in the dark panics.
4. **Protect the essentials, let the non-essentials slip, on purpose.** Under real pressure you may not get everything done. Consciously protect what matters most and let the trivial wait, communicating that, rather than dropping things at random.
5. **Keep your system current even while busy.** Capture the new things; don't let the chaos blow up your whole operation. The system is what lets you absorb a shock without losing the rest.

## Your calm is the deliverable
When everything is on fire, the founder takes their emotional cue from you. If you're visibly panicking, they panic. If you're calm, clear, and communicating ('here's what happened, here's what I'm doing, here's when I'll update you'), they trust that it's handled, and that trust is worth more than any single task. Cultivating that steadiness, real or practised, under pressure is the mark of a senior operator.

## After the fire
Once it's resolved, close the loop (confirm it's fixed) and, where useful, note what would prevent or speed up handling it next time (a backup plan, a contact, an SOP). Turning a crisis into a slightly better-prepared operation is exactly the proactive, systems-minded thinking that makes you valuable.

cards.prompt: When a crisis hits, the founder takes their emotional cue from how you handle it.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Your calm (or panic) is contagious. A clear, communicating operator makes the founder trust it's handled; a frantic one makes them panic too.
cards.whenWrong: They do. In a crisis your composure sets the tone. Calm, clear communication signals 'handled'; visible panic spreads. Your steadiness is the deliverable.

cards.prompt: Under real pressure, consciously letting trivial tasks slip (and saying so) is better than dropping things at random.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Deliberately protecting the essentials and communicating what waits beats silent random dropping. Intentional triage under pressure is the skill.
cards.whenWrong: It is better. You may not get everything done in a crisis; choosing what slips and saying so is professional, dropping things randomly and silently is not.

items.title: Handle a mid-week crisis
items.body:
Mid-simulation, two things hit at once: the website goes down during a sale, AND a major wholesale customer emails threatening to cancel a large order over a delay.
1. Write your first 30 minutes: assess, triage, the actions you take, and the holding communications.
2. Write the proactive update you send Ama.
3. Note one 'after the fire' improvement (a backup plan or SOP) you'd add.

Deliverable: the crisis-response plan, the founder update, and the improvement note.

days.title: Capturing your work as case studies
days.summary: Turn what you did into stories that win the next opportunity.

items.title: The story is what sells
items.body:
## Doing the work is not enough
You've now done a lot of real work. But work nobody knows about wins you nothing. The bridge from 'I did good work' to 'someone hires me because of it' is the case study: a clear, short story of a problem you solved. Learning to tell these well is as important as doing the work.

## The case-study formula: situation, action, result
Every strong case study (and every strong interview answer, Week 13) follows this shape:
- **Situation:** the problem or context. 'Ama's inbox had 300 unread emails and she was missing customer orders.'
- **Action:** what YOU did, specifically. 'I built a label-and-filter triage system, cleared the backlog to zero, and set up a daily processing routine and a weekly update.'
- **Result:** the outcome, ideally concrete. 'Inbox stays at zero, no orders missed since, and Ama got back ~5 hours a week.'

Situation, action, result. Short, specific, outcome-focused. That structure turns work into proof.

## Quantify where you can
Numbers make a case study credible: hours saved, backlog cleared, response time cut, tickets reduced, orders handled, a launch delivered on time. Even rough, honest figures ('cut the report time from ~90 minutes to ~20') are far more persuasive than 'made things more efficient'. Where you don't have numbers, a concrete before/after still works ('from a chaotic inbox to inbox zero, every day').

## Keep them honest and specific
A case study is only as good as its truth. Use real (or realistic, for these simulations) details and outcomes, never inflate. Specific and honest beats grand and vague every time, and you'll have to back it up in an interview. The good news: after this course you have ten real artefacts and these engagements to draw genuine case studies from, which most beginners cannot do.

## Write a few now
Turn your strongest pieces of work, the communication toolkit, an inbox transformation, the operations manual, a delivered engagement, the crisis you handled, into short situation-action-result case studies. These become the backbone of your portfolio, profile, and interview answers in Week 13.

cards.prompt: A strong case study follows situation, action, result, and quantifies the outcome where possible.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Situation-action-result with a concrete number ('saved ~5 hours/week') turns work into credible proof that wins the next opportunity.
cards.whenWrong: That's the formula. Situation, action, result, with figures where you can, is what makes a case study persuasive rather than a vague claim.

cards.prompt: It's fine to inflate the results in a case study to make it more impressive.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Never inflate, you'll have to back it up in an interview, and specific honest results beat grand vague ones. Truth is the case study's value.
cards.whenWrong: No. Inflation backfires when you can't defend it. Honest, specific outcomes are both more credible and more persuasive than exaggerated claims.

items.title: Write three case studies
items.body:
Pick three of your strongest pieces of work (from the whole course and these engagements). For each, write a short case study:
1. Situation (the problem/context).
2. Action (specifically what you did).
3. Result (the outcome, quantified or concrete before/after).

Keep each to a short paragraph, honest and specific. Deliverable: three situation-action-result case studies.

days.title: Ship: simulation complete, portfolio consolidated
days.summary: Finish the simulation and pull everything into one portfolio.

items.title: Everything, working together
items.body:
## The week's deliverable
Today you complete the founder-assistant simulation and consolidate your work: the delivered local-business project, a simulation log (how you ran the week, prioritised, switched, operated proactively, and handled the crisis), and your case studies, all pulled into one coherent portfolio of real work.

## The simulation log
Write up the simulated week honestly: what the week threw at you, how you prioritised the chaotic morning, how you handled the crisis, where you operated proactively, and what you'd do better. This reflection is not busywork, it cements the integrated skill and gives you rich, specific material for interviews ('tell me about a time you handled competing priorities under pressure', you have a real answer now).

## Consolidate the portfolio
You now have a lot: ten skill artefacts (Weeks 1 to 10) plus real engagements (startup, NGO, local business) and a founder simulation. Pull them into one organised portfolio, grouped and labelled, each with a short case-study note. This is the body of evidence Week 13 will turn into a CV, a LinkedIn profile, and a portfolio site. Organising it now means Week 13 is assembly, not scramble.

## What you've proven
Stepping back: you can communicate, organise, run an inbox and calendar, research, use AI, manage projects, run support, manage social, document operations, handle the business of remote work, AND deliver for different client types while running everything at once under pressure. That is a genuinely capable remote operations professional. The simulation is the proof that it all works together, not just as separate skills.

## The standard
Three tests: the local-business project is delivered and documented; the simulation log honestly shows you prioritising, switching, anticipating, and staying calm under pressure; and the consolidated portfolio is organised, labelled, and case-studied, ready to present. Hit those and you walk into Week 13 with everything you need to get hired or land clients.

cards.prompt: Writing an honest reflection on the simulation gives you real material for interview questions about handling pressure.
cards.whenRight: Yes. 'Tell me about a time you juggled competing priorities under pressure' now has a real, specific answer from your logged simulation. Reflection turns experience into stories.
cards.whenWrong: It does. The log becomes interview gold: concrete situation-action-result stories about prioritising and handling crises, drawn from what you actually did.

cards.prompt: Consolidating the portfolio now makes Week 13 (career launch) assembly rather than a scramble.
cards.whenRight: Yes. With artefacts organised, labelled, and case-studied, Week 13 is just assembling them into a CV, profile, and site, not hunting and writing from scratch.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Organising the evidence now means the career-launch week is smooth assembly. Leaving it scattered makes Week 13 a frantic scramble.

items.title: Final build: simulation + consolidated portfolio
items.body:
This is the Week 12 deliverable. Produce:
1. **The delivered local-business project**, documented plainly.
2. **A founder-assistant simulation log**: the week's events, how you prioritised the busy morning, handled the crisis, operated proactively, and what you'd improve.
3. **A consolidated portfolio**: all your artefacts and engagements organised, labelled, each with a short case-study note.

Keep it shareable and export key pieces as PDFs. This completes your real-context portfolio, ready for Week 13.

topics: The integrated founder-assistant role
Prioritising across competing demands (urgency x impact)
Context-switching without dropping balls
Operating proactively and anticipating needs
Delivering for a local business
Performing and communicating under pressure
Writing case studies (situation, action, result)
Consolidating a portfolio of real work
tasks: Set up your full operating system for a simulated week
Prioritise a chaotic morning by urgency and impact
Context-switch cleanly with captured open threads
Practise proactive anticipation with decision-points
Deliver a practical local-business project
Handle a mid-week crisis calmly and communicate it
Write situation-action-result case studies and consolidate the portfolio
weeks.project: Complete the local-business project and a founder-assistant simulation: operate as Ama's right hand for a simulated week, handling a live mix of inbox, calendar, tasks, research, support, and reporting plus a crisis, while delivering a local-business engagement in parallel. Capture it all as case studies and a consolidated portfolio.
exercises: Prioritise a chaotic morning with reasons and holding replies
Write switch-notes through a context-switching sequence
Write four proactive moves with their decision-points
Deliver a practical local-business project with plain documentation
Write a crisis-response plan, a founder update, and three case studies
questions: How do you prioritise when everything feels urgent?
What does operating proactively look like in practice?
How do you keep quality high while context-switching?
outputs: A consolidated, presentable portfolio of real work
mastery_questions: Prioritise a list of competing tasks by urgency and impact and justify the order
Send holding replies that make triaged-aside tasks feel handled, not ignored
Capture an open thread before switching tasks so nothing is dropped
Identify a proactive move you'd make before being asked, and its decision-point
Deliver a practical local-business project with non-technical documentation
Run a simulated busy day handling inbox, calendar, tasks, and support together
Respond to a mid-week crisis: assess, triage, act, and communicate calmly
Write a situation-action-result case study with a quantified or concrete result
Consolidate artefacts and engagements into an organised, labelled portfolio
Reflect on a simulated week and name your two biggest growth areas
weeks.ai_assist: Use AI as your operating partner during the simulation: rapid drafting, summarising long threads, converting time zones, turning your notes into reports and case studies. Ask it to draft a situation-action-result case study from your bullet points, then make it honest and specific. The simulation tests whether you can run real operations fast and well under pressure; AI is part of how a modern operator moves quickly. Own every output, and keep your judgement, especially the prioritisation and the crisis calls, firmly human.
weeks.pre_flight: Before the simulation, set up your daily plan and your capture system so nothing gets lost when things get busy. The operators who stay calm under load are the ones whose system catches the balls, not their memory. Decide in advance how you'll triage and how often you'll update the founder.
common_mistakes: Reacting to whatever is loudest instead of what matters most
Letting one urgent fire cause three other things to slip silently
Only doing what is asked, never anticipating what's next
Panicking visibly in a crisis instead of communicating calm control
Finishing the work but never packaging it as case studies
weeks.debug_help: If the simulation feels overwhelming, that is the point, and the fix is the system, not heroics. Triage by urgency and impact, communicate what will wait, and trust your capture system to hold everything. If you keep dropping things when switching, you're relying on memory, note the open thread before every switch. If a crisis rattles you, slow down ten seconds to assess before acting, and remember the founder takes their cue from your calm. Calm, communicated triage under pressure is exactly the skill being tested.
stretch: Add a fourth engagement type you haven't tried yet
Get a testimonial or reference from a real or mentor 'client'
Record a short video walkthrough of your consolidated portfolio

weeks.title: Career launchpad
weeks.context:
You have the skills and you have the proof: ten portfolio artefacts and real engagements with a startup, an NGO, and a local business. This final week turns all of that into income. You will build a results-focused CV, an optimised LinkedIn profile, a portfolio site, an interview-preparation pack, and a concrete 30-day plan to land work. By the end, you are not 'someone who studied this'; you are a remote operations professional with everything packaged and ready to send.

The whole course was building to this. A student who finishes this week can apply for remote roles, pitch freelance clients, and present themselves credibly, with evidence, not adjectives. The goal of the track, employable or earning within weeks, is met here.

The thread through this week: everywhere, lead with evidence and results, not claims. You have done real work. Your job now is to make that undeniable to anyone who looks.

concept_check.q: Which CV bullet is stronger?
choices: 'Responsible for managing email and calendar.'
'Took a founder's 300-email backlog to inbox zero and built a system that saved ~5 hours/week.'
'Hardworking and detail-oriented team player.'
'Did various admin tasks.'
concept_check.explain: Show results, not duties. A bullet with a concrete outcome (backlog cleared, hours saved) proves capability; listing responsibilities or adjectives proves nothing.

concept_check.q: What is the most important thing a portfolio should do?
choices: List every tool you've heard of
Show real work with the outcome it produced, so a client can see you can actually do the job
Look flashy with lots of graphics
Be as long as possible
concept_check.explain: A portfolio is proof. Real artefacts plus the result each produced answer the only question a client has: can this person do the job? Tool lists and flash do not.

concept_check.q: You finish the course with a great portfolio but send zero applications or pitches. What happens?
choices: Clients find you automatically
Nothing, the work and the portfolio only pay off when you actually reach out and apply
Your LinkedIn does all the work
You should wait to feel ready
concept_check.explain: The most common failure after a course is never actually applying or pitching. Skills and a portfolio are potential; reaching out, consistently, is what converts them to income.

days.title: Turning skills into income, and gather your evidence
days.summary: Understand how the pieces convert to work, then assemble all your proof in one place.

items.title: From capable to hired
items.body:
## The final conversion
Everything until now made you capable and gave you proof. This week converts that into actual work. The pieces fit together: your portfolio is the evidence, your CV and LinkedIn present it for roles, your portfolio site presents it for clients, interview prep wins the conversation, and your acquisition plan is how you reach the people who'll hire you. Build all five this week and you are ready to earn.

## Two routes, one foundation
You can pursue remote employment (a role with one company) or freelancing/clients (one or several), and most people mix them. Both run on the same foundation you've built: real skills, a portfolio of proof, and the ability to present yourself credibly. The CV and LinkedIn lean toward roles; the portfolio site and outreach lean toward clients; all of them rest on your evidence.

## The golden rule of this week: evidence over adjectives
'Hardworking, detail-oriented, passionate' are words anyone can type, and they convince no one. 'Took an inbox to zero and saved 5 hours/week', 'ran a support queue and cut repeat tickets', 'delivered a launch on time', these are evidence, and they convince everyone. Every artefact this week, the CV, the profile, the portfolio, the interview answers, should lead with what you actually did and the result. You have the evidence; this week is about presenting it relentlessly.

## This week's destination
A complete, ready-to-send career package: CV, LinkedIn, portfolio site, interview prep, and a 30-day action plan. After this, the only thing between you and income is hitting send, which is exactly what the 30-day plan makes you do.

items.title: How to Optimize LinkedIn Profile to Land Your Dream Job in 2026
items.creator: Cindy Dodd
items.why: A concise, practical walk through optimising every part of a LinkedIn profile, the exact moves you'll apply on Day 2. Watch it now for the overview, then build your own profile this week.

items.title: Gather all your evidence, step by step
items.body:
## Assemble before you build
Before writing a CV or profile, gather your raw material in one place, so every document you build this week pulls from the same evidence rather than starting from a blank page.

**1. List every artefact.** Your ten portfolio pieces (communication toolkit, digital workspace, inbox/calendar SOP, research package, AI operations system, project package, support simulation, social content month, operations manual, remote-work setup) plus your real engagements (startup, NGO, local business) and the founder simulation.

**2. List every concrete result.** From your Week 12 case studies and your work: hours saved, backlogs cleared, tickets reduced, launches delivered, systems built, customers handled. Write the numbers and concrete before/afters down. These become your CV bullets, profile highlights, and interview answers.

**3. List your skills and tools.** Everything you can now do (communication, inbox/calendar, research, AI, project management, support, social, SOPs/operations, remote-work setup) and the tools you've used (Gmail/Workspace, Notion, Trello, Canva, ChatGPT/Claude, Buffer, Calendly, etc.). This is your skills section.

**4. Decide your positioning.** From Week 10: who you serve and what you do, in one line. 'Remote operations professional helping founders and small teams run their back office.' This headline threads through everything.

## Why this step matters
Most people write a CV by staring at a blank page and inventing generic phrases. You'll write yours by selecting from a list of real things you did and real results you produced. That is why your materials will be specific and credible where others are vague, you're working from evidence, and you have more of it than most beginners ever assemble.

cards.prompt: The golden rule for every career document this week is to lead with evidence and results, not adjectives.
cards.whenRight: Yes. 'Saved 5 hours/week' convinces; 'hardworking and passionate' does not. You have the evidence, so present it relentlessly across CV, profile, and portfolio.
cards.whenWrong: Evidence over adjectives is the rule. Anyone can claim qualities; concrete results and real work are what actually persuade a client or employer.

cards.prompt: Gathering all your artefacts, results, and skills first makes writing the CV and profile easier and more specific.
cards.whenRight: Yes. You write by selecting from real evidence, not staring at a blank page, which is exactly why your materials come out specific and credible.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Assembling the evidence first means every document pulls from real work, producing specific, credible materials instead of generic phrases.

items.title: Your turn, gather the evidence
items.body:
Build a single 'evidence doc' with four sections:
- [ ] Every artefact and engagement you completed
- [ ] Every concrete result (numbers and before/afters from your case studies)
- [ ] Your skills and the tools you've used
- [ ] Your one-line positioning (who you serve + what you do)

Deliverable: the evidence doc, the source you'll build everything else from.

days.title: The results-focused CV
days.summary: A CV that proves you can do the job, not just that you held one.

items.title: Write a CV that gets a reply
items.body:
## What a CV is for
A CV's one job is to get you to the next step (a reply, an interview). A recruiter or founder skims it in seconds, so it must communicate fast: who you are, what you can do, and the proof, at a glance. Most CVs fail by listing duties; yours will win by showing results.

## The structure
- **Header:** name, a one-line title/positioning ('Remote Operations Professional | inbox, calendar, projects, support'), and contact (professional email, LinkedIn, portfolio link).
- **Summary:** 2 to 3 lines, who you are and the value you bring, with a concrete hook. Lead with what you do for an employer/client.
- **Experience / projects:** this is where, with limited paid experience, your course work shines. Frame your engagements and portfolio projects as experience: 'Remote Operations (project-based / training engagements)' with results-focused bullets.
- **Skills:** the concrete capabilities and tools from your evidence doc.
- **Education / certifications:** including this Forge track.

## Results-focused bullets
The heart of a strong CV. Each bullet shows an action and a result, not a duty:
- Weak: 'Responsible for email management.'
- Strong: 'Cleared a 300-email backlog to inbox zero and built a triage system that saved ~5 hours/week.'
- Weak: 'Handled customer service.'
- Strong: 'Resolved a 15-ticket support queue, de-escalated escalations, and proposed fixes that cut repeat tickets.'

Start each with a strong verb (Built, Cleared, Delivered, Resolved, Coordinated, Reduced) and end with the outcome. Pull these straight from your case studies.

## Keep it clean and tailored
One or two pages, clean and scannable (your Week 2 and Canva skills apply), no typos (proofread, and use Grammarly). And tailor it: adjust the summary and emphasis to match a specific role when you apply. A CV aimed at everyone speaks to no one; a lightly tailored one shows you're a fit.

cards.prompt: With limited paid experience, your portfolio projects and engagements can be framed as experience on your CV.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Real project work is real experience. Frame your engagements and portfolio pieces with results-focused bullets, you have more proof than most beginners.
cards.whenWrong: They can. Project-based and training engagements are legitimate experience. Present them with results-focused bullets rather than leaving the section bare.

cards.prompt: A CV bullet should start with a strong action verb and end with the outcome.
cards.whenRight: Yes. 'Built X that saved Y' beats 'Responsible for X'. Verb-first, result-last bullets prove capability fast to a skimming reader.
cards.whenWrong: That's the formula. Lead with a strong verb (Built, Cleared, Delivered) and close with the concrete result, so each bullet shows impact, not just duty.

items.title: Write your CV
items.body:
Using your evidence doc, write a one-to-two page CV:
1. Header with positioning and contact (incl. portfolio + LinkedIn).
2. A 2 to 3 line summary leading with your value.
3. An experience/projects section with at least 5 results-focused bullets (verb-first, outcome-last) drawn from your case studies.
4. Skills/tools and education (incl. this track).

Build it in Google Docs or a clean Canva CV template. Deliverable: your CV (PDF).

days.title: LinkedIn optimisation
days.summary: A profile that finds you opportunities and earns trust.

items.title: Make LinkedIn work for you
items.body:
## Why LinkedIn matters
LinkedIn is where remote employers and many clients check you out, and increasingly where they find you. A strong profile does double duty: it convinces someone you sent a proposal to, and it gets you discovered by people searching for what you offer. Treat it as your always-on storefront.

## Optimise the key sections
- **Photo and banner:** your professional headshot (Week 1) and a simple banner. First impression in a glance.
- **Headline:** the most important line. Not just 'Virtual Assistant' but who you help and how: 'Remote Operations Professional | I help founders and small teams run their inbox, calendar, projects and support'. This is what shows in search and feeds, and it's prime real estate, use it to state your value.
- **About:** a few short paragraphs in first person and your voice: what you do, who you help, the results you create, and a clear call to action ('open to remote operations roles / freelance clients, message me or see my portfolio at [link]'). Scannable, specific, human.
- **Experience:** mirror your CV, your engagements and projects framed with results.
- **Skills:** add the relevant ones (LinkedIn uses these in search); pin your top few.
- **Featured:** link your portfolio pieces and site here, so proof is one click away.

## Searchability
LinkedIn is a search engine. Use the words people search for (the role titles and skills, 'executive assistant', 'operations', 'customer support', 'social media management') naturally in your headline, about, and skills, so you appear when someone looks for what you do.

## Be visible, not just present
A complete profile is the foundation; a little activity multiplies it. Posting occasionally (a project you shipped, a lesson learned, your case studies reworked as posts) and engaging thoughtfully on others' posts keeps you visible and builds your reputation over time. You don't need to be an influencer, just not invisible. Even modest, consistent presence puts you ahead of the silent majority.

## Connect with intent
Grow your network deliberately: founders, others in remote ops, people in industries you want to serve. A warm, personalised connection note ('I help founders run their operations, would love to connect') beats blank requests. Your network is, over time, your best source of work (Week 10).

cards.prompt: Your LinkedIn headline should state who you help and how, not just your job title.
cards.whenRight: Yes. The headline is prime real estate and shows in search and feeds. 'I help founders run their inbox, projects and support' beats a bare title.
cards.whenWrong: It should. A value-focused headline gets you found and understood; a bare title wastes the most visible line on your profile.

cards.prompt: LinkedIn works partly as a search engine, so using the words people search for helps you get found.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Naturally including the role titles and skills people search ('operations', 'executive assistant', 'customer support') in your profile makes you appear in their results.
cards.whenWrong: It does. LinkedIn surfaces profiles by keywords, so weaving the terms people actually search into your headline, about, and skills makes you discoverable.

items.title: Optimise your LinkedIn profile
items.body:
Build or overhaul your LinkedIn profile:
1. Set the professional photo and a simple banner.
2. Write a value-focused headline (who you help + how, with searchable terms).
3. Write an 'About' in your voice with a clear call to action.
4. Add experience (mirroring your CV), skills, and link portfolio pieces in Featured.

Deliverable: the live profile (or a screenshot/draft of each section).

days.title: Building a portfolio site
days.summary: One link that shows everything you can do.

items.title: Your portfolio, on one link
items.body:
## Why a portfolio site
A CV tells; a portfolio shows. A simple portfolio site (or page) gives you one link to send anyone, a client, an employer, a connection, that displays your real work and the results it produced. For a remote operations professional, it's powerful precisely because most VAs don't have one; it instantly sets you apart.

## You don't need to code
Build it with free, no-code tools: a Notion page (made public), a Canva website, a Google Site, or a simple site builder. The tool doesn't matter; clarity does. Even a single well-organised public Notion page works beautifully and takes an afternoon.

## What it should contain
- **A clear top:** your name, your positioning line, and a one-line intro. The visitor should instantly know who you are and what you do.
- **Your work, as case studies:** your strongest pieces, each shown as situation-action-result with the artefact linked or pictured. Lead with results. Group them sensibly (communication, operations, support, social, etc.).
- **Services (for clients):** your packages from Week 10, so a client knows what they can hire you for.
- **About:** a short, human paragraph and your photo.
- **Contact / call to action:** how to reach you and a clear next step ('Email me / book a call to talk about your operations').

## Curate, don't dump
Show your best work, not everything. A focused portfolio of strong, well-presented pieces beats a cluttered dump. Each piece should make the visitor think 'I want this person handling that for me'. Quality and clarity over volume, the same lesson as the whole course.

## Keep it real and current
Use your actual work (the simulations and engagements are legitimate, present them honestly), and update it as you do real client work. A living portfolio that grows with each engagement becomes a more and more powerful asset, and the habit of capturing each project as a case study (Week 12) keeps it fed.

cards.prompt: You need coding skills to build a portfolio site.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Free no-code tools (a public Notion page, Canva site, Google Sites) work great. Even a single well-organised Notion page is enough. Clarity matters, not code.
cards.whenWrong: You don't. No-code tools build a clean portfolio in an afternoon. The content and clarity matter far more than any technical skill.

cards.prompt: A portfolio should show your best, curated work rather than everything you've ever done.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Curate. A focused set of strong, well-presented pieces beats a cluttered dump, each one should make the visitor want to hire you for that.
cards.whenWrong: Curate it. Showing everything dilutes impact. A tight selection of your best work, presented as results, is far more persuasive than a pile.

items.title: Build your portfolio site
items.body:
Build a simple portfolio (public Notion page, Canva site, or Google Site):
1. A clear top: name, positioning, one-line intro.
2. 4 to 6 of your best pieces as case studies (situation-action-result, with the work linked/shown).
3. Your services/packages (from Week 10) and a short About with your photo.
4. A clear contact + call to action.

Deliverable: the live portfolio link.

days.title: Interview preparation
days.summary: Walk into any conversation able to prove you're the one.

items.title: Win the conversation
items.body:
## The interview (or discovery call)
Whether it's a formal job interview or a client discovery call (Week 10), the goal is the same: show you understand their need and can deliver. Preparation is what turns nerves into confidence, and you now have real work to draw on, which most candidates for these roles don't.

## Prepare your stories
Most interview questions are answered best with a specific story in the situation-action-result shape (Week 12). Prepare a handful from your work:
- A time you organised chaos (the inbox/operations work).
- A time you handled a difficult customer or person (de-escalation).
- A time you juggled competing priorities under pressure (the simulation).
- A time you took initiative / anticipated a need (proactivity).
- A time you fixed or improved a process (SOPs / efficiency).

With these ready, you can answer almost any behavioural question ('tell me about a time...') with a concrete, credible story instead of a vague generalisation.

## Common questions to rehearse
- 'Tell me about yourself' (a 60-second pitch: who you are, what you do, the value you bring, lead with positioning, not life story).
- 'Why should we hire you / why are you a fit?' (their need + your matching evidence).
- 'What's your experience with [task/tool]?' (point to a specific thing you did).
- 'How do you handle [a hard situation]?' (a real story).
- 'What are your rates / expectations?' (know your number, Week 10).

## Research and ask questions
Before any interview, research them (Week 4 skills): the company, the role, the person. Then prepare smart questions to ask them, this shows interest and judgement, and helps you assess fit. 'What would make someone successful in this role in the first 90 days?' is a strong one. An interview is a two-way conversation, not an interrogation.

## Logistics and presence
For remote interviews: test your tech, find a quiet space with decent light, be early, and bring the same warm-and-competent presence you've practised all course. Have your portfolio open to reference. And remember, you've done the work; you're not begging for a chance, you're showing a fit. That mindset reads as quiet confidence, which is exactly what wins these roles.

cards.prompt: Most behavioural interview questions are best answered with a specific situation-action-result story.
cards.whenRight: Yes. 'Tell me about a time...' wants a concrete story. Prepare a handful from your real work and you can answer almost any of them credibly.
cards.whenWrong: They are. A specific story (situation, action, result) beats a vague generalisation every time, and you now have real ones to tell.

cards.prompt: Preparing thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer is a waste of time.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Good questions show interest and judgement and help you assess fit. An interview is a two-way conversation; asking well is part of impressing them.
cards.whenWrong: It's valuable. Smart questions signal interest and judgement and help you evaluate the role. Going in with none is a missed chance to stand out.

items.title: Prepare your interview pack
items.body:
1. Write your 60-second 'tell me about yourself'.
2. Prepare 5 situation-action-result stories (chaos organised, difficult person handled, priorities under pressure, initiative taken, process improved).
3. Write answers to 'why should we hire you?' and 'how do you handle competing deadlines?'.
4. Write 4 smart questions to ask an interviewer/client.

Deliverable: the interview-prep pack.

days.title: Client acquisition and outreach
days.summary: Actually reach the people who will hire you.

items.title: Going and getting the work
items.body:
## The step most people skip
Here's the uncomfortable truth: most people finish a course, build a portfolio, and then wait, and nothing happens. Clients and jobs do not arrive on their own. The work comes from you reaching out, consistently. This day is about doing the thing that actually produces income.

## The channels (from Week 10, now activated)
- **Apply to roles:** remote job boards and platforms, with your tailored CV and a short, problem-led cover note. Apply to fits, focused, not spray.
- **Freelance platforms:** set up your Upwork profile and send tailored proposals to well-matched jobs.
- **Direct outreach:** the highest-leverage and most-avoided. Identify businesses that need help (your Week 4 prospecting), and reach out with a warm, specific message that leads with their problem and your relevant proof.
- **Your network:** tell people what you do. Post on LinkedIn that you're available. Ask anyone who knows your work for referrals. Warm leads convert best.

## The outreach message
A cold outreach that works is short, about them, and specific:
- Open with their situation or a genuine observation ('I saw your shop is growing fast, congrats').
- Name the problem you can solve ('founders at that stage usually drown in admin and customer messages').
- Offer specific value and proof ('I set up operations systems that take that off your plate, here's an example: [link]').
- Make the next step easy and low-pressure ('open to a quick call to see if I can help? No pressure either way').

Personalise every one. Generic blasts get ignored; a message that clearly speaks to them gets replies.

## Volume, consistency, and a thick skin
Acquisition is a numbers game with a skill on top. Not everyone replies; that's normal, not failure. The people who land work are the ones who reach out consistently, learn from what works, and don't take silence personally. A daily or weekly outreach habit (e.g. 5 quality applications/messages a day) compounds. Track your outreach (a simple sheet: who, when, status, follow-up) so you follow up, most work comes after a polite second contact, not the first.

## The de-risking offer (again)
For a first client unsure about you, the paid trial from Week 10 is your friend: a small, low-commitment piece of work that lets your real delivery prove itself. Many first clients are won this way. Get one happy client and the referrals and reviews begin to compound.

cards.prompt: After finishing the course, clients and jobs will generally come to you without you reaching out.
cards.whenRight: Correct. This is the big trap. Skills and a portfolio are potential; consistent outreach and applications are what actually produce income. You have to go get it.
cards.whenWrong: They won't. Waiting is why most people never earn from their skills. The work comes from reaching out consistently, not from being discovered passively.

cards.prompt: Tracking your outreach and following up tends to win more work than relying on the first contact alone.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Most work comes after a polite follow-up, not the first message. Tracking who/when/status means you actually follow up instead of forgetting.
cards.whenWrong: It does. A second, polite contact converts a lot of leads the first one didn't. A simple tracker is what makes consistent follow-up happen.

items.title: Start acquiring
items.body:
1. Build a target list of 20 potential clients or employers (real ones, using Week 4 prospecting).
2. Write a personalised cold outreach message (their situation, the problem, your value + proof, an easy next step).
3. Set up an outreach tracker (who, when, channel, status, follow-up).
4. Actually send at least 3 applications or outreach messages this week.

Deliverable: the target list, the outreach message, the tracker, and proof you sent at least 3.

days.title: Personal brand and your 30-day plan
days.summary: Position yourself clearly, and commit to a concrete plan to land work.

items.title: Positioning and a plan you'll actually follow
items.body:
## Personal brand, simply
Your 'personal brand' is just what people reliably associate with you, the clear, consistent answer to 'what does this person do and how well?'. You don't need to be an influencer. You need consistency: the same positioning, the same professional quality, the same voice across your CV, LinkedIn, portfolio, and outreach. When everything points the same way, you become memorable and credible. Pick your positioning (Week 10) and make everything echo it.

## Reputation is built by delivery
The strongest brand-builder is simply doing excellent work and letting it spread, through testimonials, referrals, repeat clients, and case studies. Early on, every client is also a brand-building opportunity: deliver brilliantly, ask happy clients for a testimonial and a referral, and turn each engagement into a case study. Over a year, this compounds into a reputation that brings work to you.

## The 30-day plan
A goal without a plan is a wish. Before you finish, write a concrete 30-day plan to land your first role or client(s). Make it specific and action-based, for example:
- **Week 1:** finalise CV, LinkedIn, and portfolio; set up Upwork; build a target list of 20.
- **Week 2:** apply to 10 roles and send 10 tailored proposals/outreach; post once on LinkedIn that you're available.
- **Week 3:** follow up on everything; send 10 more; do any interviews/calls; offer a paid trial where it fits.
- **Week 4:** keep the outreach habit; refine based on what's getting replies; aim to close a first client/role or paid trial.

Set a daily or weekly target (e.g. 5 quality outreaches/applications a day) and a way to track it. The plan's job is to make sure you act, consistently, instead of stalling.

## Beat the 'not ready yet' trap
The biggest risk now is your own hesitation, waiting to feel 'ready', polishing forever, fearing rejection. You are ready: you have skills and proof most beginners never assemble. Done and out-there beats perfect and hidden. The 30-day plan exists to push you past hesitation into action, because action is the only thing that turns this entire course into income.

## You've come a long way
From Week 1's first email to here: you can run a founder's operations end to end, and you have the portfolio to prove it. The next concrete thing is simple, execute the plan and reach out. That's how this becomes a livelihood.

cards.prompt: A personal brand mainly requires becoming an influencer with a big following.
cards.whenRight: Correct. It just requires consistency, the same positioning, quality, and voice everywhere, plus excellent delivery that earns testimonials and referrals. No influencing needed.
cards.whenWrong: Not at all. A personal brand is consistency plus great work, not follower count. Aligning your positioning everywhere and delivering well is what builds it.

cards.prompt: The biggest risk after finishing the course is waiting to feel 'ready' instead of taking action.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Hesitation and over-polishing are the real enemies now. You have skills and proof; done-and-out-there beats perfect-and-hidden. The 30-day plan exists to push you to act.
cards.whenWrong: It is. The 'not ready yet' trap stops more graduates than any skill gap. You're ready, the plan's job is to make you act despite the hesitation.

items.title: Write your 30-day plan
items.body:
1. Write your one-line positioning and check your CV, LinkedIn, and portfolio all echo it.
2. Write a concrete 30-day plan (week by week) to land your first role/client, with specific weekly actions.
3. Set a daily or weekly outreach target and how you'll track it.
4. Write one sentence committing to start (a date you'll send your first applications).

Deliverable: the 30-day plan with positioning, weekly actions, target, and start commitment.

days.title: Ship: your complete career package
days.summary: Assemble everything into a ready-to-send package. The capstone.

items.title: Ready to earn
items.body:
## The final deliverable
Today you assemble your complete career package: CV, optimised LinkedIn, portfolio site, interview-prep pack, and 30-day plan, all consistent, all leading with evidence, all ready to send. This is the capstone of the whole track. With it, you are a remote operations professional equipped to land work.

## What 'done' means
Each piece should pass a test:
- **CV:** results-focused, clean, tailored-ready, no typos.
- **LinkedIn:** value-headline, strong about, work and proof linked, searchable.
- **Portfolio:** one link, best work as case studies, services, clear contact.
- **Interview pack:** a 60-second pitch and five real stories ready.
- **30-day plan:** specific weekly actions and a start date.

And they all point the same way, same positioning, same quality, same person.

## The meta-test of the whole course
The real test is the track's promise: a graduate who can secure remote work, internships, freelance opportunities, assistant roles, operations roles, or entry-level international employment without needing more training. Look at what you're holding, real skills across ten domains, a portfolio of real artefacts and engagements, and a complete, evidenced career package. That promise is met. The only thing left is to execute your plan.

## Then: go
Finish the package, then start the 30-day plan, today if you can. Send the first applications, the first proposals, the first outreach. Everything in this course was preparation for that action. The next concrete thing is to reach out, and that's how all of this becomes income, and a career.

cards.prompt: The pieces of your career package should all point the same way: consistent positioning, quality, and voice.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Consistency across CV, LinkedIn, portfolio, and outreach is what makes you credible and memorable. They should clearly be one professional, telling one story.
cards.whenWrong: They should align. A consistent positioning and quality across every piece is what builds credibility; mixed messages dilute it.

cards.prompt: Once the career package is built, the final and most important action is to execute the plan and reach out.
cards.whenRight: Yes. The package is preparation; the outreach is what produces income. Everything in the course was building to the action of reaching out, so go do it.
cards.whenWrong: It is. A finished package that never gets sent earns nothing. Executing the 30-day plan, applying and reaching out, is the step that turns it all into a career.

items.title: Final build: the complete career package
items.body:
This is the Week 13 capstone deliverable. Assemble and finalise:
1. **Your CV** (results-focused, PDF).
2. **Your optimised LinkedIn profile** (live).
3. **Your portfolio site** (one shareable link, best work as case studies).
4. **Your interview-prep pack** (pitch + 5 stories + questions).
5. **Your 30-day action plan** with a start date.

Check everything is consistent and leads with evidence. Then begin the plan: send your first 3 applications or outreach messages. This is your graduation deliverable as a Remote Operations Professional.

weeks.ai_assist: Use AI to draft and sharpen every piece, CV bullets, LinkedIn copy, portfolio case-study notes, outreach messages, and to interview you with hard questions and critique your answers. Feed it your evidence doc so it works from your real results, not generic phrases. Then make everything unmistakably yours: the final presentation of you should sound like you at your most clear and confident, never like generic AI copy a recruiter has seen a hundred times. The decisions, your positioning, your rate, who you target, stay yours.
weeks.pre_flight: Before writing your CV and profile, complete the evidence doc: list every concrete result from your projects and engagements (hours saved, backlogs cleared, customers handled, deliverables shipped). Your materials should be built from this real evidence, not adjectives. If a section feels weak, the fix is almost always a missing specific result you can pull from your case studies.
common_mistakes: A CV that lists duties instead of results
A LinkedIn profile that is a bare job-title list with no positioning or proof
A portfolio that shows work with no context on the outcome it produced
Polishing forever and waiting to feel 'ready' instead of reaching out
Finishing the package but never actually sending an application or pitch
weeks.debug_help: If your materials feel weak, the fix is almost always specificity: replace 'managed social media' with 'planned and ran a 30-day content calendar that did X'. You have the evidence from this whole course, use it. If you're not getting replies, check whether your outreach is tailored and problem-led with proof, or generic; and whether you're following up (most work comes from the second contact). And if you find yourself stalling to feel 'ready', that's the real blocker, not a skill gap: set a start date, send three messages, and let momentum build.
